Graph theory

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Foundations of mathematics
OurBigBook.com Words: 49k Articles: 693
Graph theory studies vertices and the edges connecting them: which graph paths exist, how efficiently we can travel, and which connections are indispensable. A road map becomes a graph when junctions are vertices and road segments are edges; a communications network uses routers and links instead. The drawing helps us see connections, but its apparent lengths need not be the costs being optimized. Record travel times or transmission costs separately in a weighted graph.
The appeal of graph theory is that one model serves many practical questions. Graph paths describe routes, connected components of a graph identify isolated regions, and minimum spanning trees connect all locations cheaply. The shortest path problem asks a different question: find the cheapest journey between specified locations. Our four-vertex example below makes that distinction concrete and shows how the Dijkstra algorithm discovers a route without trying every graph path.

Geometric spanner (dG​(u,v)≤t∥u−v∥)

Words: 90
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A geometric spanner is a weighted graph on points in Euclidean space, with edge weights equal to their Euclidean distances, in which every pair has a graph path of length at most t times its direct distance. Its stretch factor is the largest ratio dG​(u,v)/∥u−v∥, where dG​ is shortest-path distance. A square's four perimeter edges, without diagonals, give stretch factor 2​: adjacent points have ratio one, and diagonal pairs have route length 2 instead of 2​. The aim is to retain short routes with fewer edges than a complete graph. [ref].

Here excess means edges minus vertices. For a connected graph it is one less than the number of independent cycles. Deleting a leaf and its incident edge, or suppressing a degree-two vertex, preserves excess. This convention differs by one from the cyclomatic number for connected graphs.

Bicyclic kernel classification

Words: 77
Bicyclic graph OurBigBook.com
The graph kernel of a bicyclic graph satisfies ∑v​(degv−2)=2, with all degrees at least three. It therefore has either one degree-four vertex carrying two loops, a bouquet graph, or two degree-three vertices. In the latter case connectivity and degree counting give either three parallel edges, the three-edge Theta graph, or one edge between the vertices and one loop at each, a dumbbell graph. All bicyclic cores are subdivisions of these three kernels, subject to simplicity restrictions on loop lengths and parallel paths.

2-core of a graph (C2​(G))

Words: 123 Articles: 1
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The 2-core is the unique largest induced subgraph with minimum degree at least two. It is obtained by repeatedly deleting vertices of degree zero or one. Every subgraph with minimum degree two survives each deletion, which proves maximality and order independence. In a connected graph with a nonempty 2-core, the deleted vertices form rooted trees attached individually to the core vertices.

Graph kernel (K(G))

Words: 67
2-core of a graph OurBigBook.com
For a connected graph whose 2-core contains a vertex of degree at least three, suppress each maximal path with degree-two internal vertices to a single edge, allowing its two endpoints to coincide. The resulting multigraph, retaining loops and parallel edges, is its kernel. Suppression preserves graph excess and leaves minimum degree at least three. A purely cyclic core is a separate unicyclic case; it has no branching vertex to anchor this construction.

Chordal graph

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A chordal graph is a finite simple graph with no induced cycle of length at least four. Equivalently, every cycle in a graph with at least four vertices has a chord: an edge joining two nonconsecutive vertices of that graph cycle. The word "induced" matters: the induced subgraph on the chosen vertices must contain exactly the cycle's edges, with no chords. Triangles are allowed. This definition concerns adjacency, independently of how the graph is drawn.
For the square cycle graph C4​, take vertex set {a,b,c,d} and set of edges {ab,bc,cd,da}, where ab abbreviates {a,b}. Its graph neighbourhoods are N(a)=N(c)={b,d} and N(b)=N(d)={a,c}. The square is an induced cycle, so C4​ is not a chordal graph. Add the single edge ac: now N(a)={b,c,d}, N(b)={a,c}, N(c)={a,b,d}, and N(d)={a,c}. The only possible four-vertex graph cycle has chord ac, so this new graph is a chordal graph. Its maximal cliques are exactly {a,b,c} and {a,c,d}.
Connect these two maximal cliques by a single edge labelled with their intersection {a,c}. The result is a junction tree, also called a clique tree: its nodes are maximal cliques, and the nodes containing any fixed original vertex induce a connected graph inside the tree. Here a,c occur in both nodes, while b,d each occur in just one. This is the running intersection property. More generally, a nonempty connected graph is a chordal graph exactly when its maximal cliques admit such a tree; a disconnected chordal graph can be represented by one such tree per connected component of a graph.[ref]
A chordal graph need not be a planar graph: the complete graph K5​ is a chordal graph, since every pair of distinct vertices is adjacent, but its ten edges violate the planar graph edge bound ∣E∣≤3∣V∣−6=9. Conversely, even a plane drawing whose bounded faces are triangles can hide an induced cycle: a wheel graph with a four-vertex rim and a central vertex joined to the whole rim still has the rim as an induced cycle. Adding chords to obtain a chordal graph is called triangulation of an undirected graph; this is an adjacency condition, rather than a requirement about planar faces.
Why is this structure useful? The maximal cliques collect local interactions, and the running intersection property makes their overlaps sufficient for consistent communication. For random variables xa​,xb​,xc​,xd​ with finite state sets, a probabilistic graphical model of the square-plus-diagonal form can have
p(xa​,xb​,xc​,xd​)=Z−1ψabc​(xa​,xb​,xc​)ψacd​(xa​,xc​,xd​),
(1)
where the two nonnegative clique potentials have a positive normalizing constant Z. Eliminating xb​ produces the two-variable junction-tree sum-product message
m(xa​,xc​)=∑xb​​ψabc​(xa​,xb​,xc​),Z=∑xa​,xc​,xd​​m(xa​,xc​)ψacd​(xa​,xc​,xd​).
(2)
The shared clique {a,c} carries everything needed from the eliminated side. For q possible states per random variable, this example uses two sums over q3 configurations after reusing the message, rather than directly summing over q4 configurations. The example's message is an exact finite sum, with no simulated data. Large maximal cliques still make exact inference expensive; chordal graphs provide a decomposition, not a universal guarantee of cheap inference.[ref]

Triangulation of an undirected graph

Words: 52
Chordal graph OurBigBook.com
Triangulation adds fill edges to an undirected graph to make it a chordal graph. Given an elimination ordering, join all remaining neighbors of each removed vertex. The completed graph has that perfect elimination ordering. Fill edges can enlarge the cliques used for exact probabilistic graphical model inference, without changing the original probability factors; they do not assert new biological relationships.

Perfect elimination ordering

Words: 683 Articles: 2
Chordal graph OurBigBook.com
A perfect elimination ordering of a finite simple graph G=(V,E) is a permutation (v1​,…,vn​) of its vertices such that each set of later graph neighbours
Ni+​={vj​:j>i, {vi​,vj​}∈E}
(3)
is a clique. Thus vi​ is a simplicial vertex in the remaining induced subgraph G[{vi​,…,vn​}]. Empty and one-vertex sets satisfy the clique condition automatically. The order here is the order of deletion: v1​ goes first.
The characterization is powerful: a finite simple graph is a chordal graph if and only if it has a perfect elimination ordering. For one proof outline, the earliest vertex of an induced cycle of length at least four would have two later graph neighbours on that graph cycle that are not adjacent, contradicting the clique condition. Conversely, every nonempty chordal graph has a simplicial vertex, and every induced subgraph of a chordal graph is a chordal graph; repeatedly deleting such a vertex supplies the ordering.[ref]
In the square-plus-diagonal chordal graph above, (b,d,a,c) is a perfect elimination ordering, with later graph neighbourhoods {a,c}, {a,c}, {c}, and ∅. Starting instead with a fails: its graph neighbours b,c,d do not form a clique, because bd is absent. Thus even a chordal graph can have a poor elimination ordering.
For a larger example, join three triangles along shared edges, using
V={a,b,c,d,e},E={ab,ac,bc,bd,cd,ce,de}.
(4)
The exact graph neighbourhoods are N(a)={b,c}, N(b)={a,c,d}, N(c)={a,b,d,e}, N(d)={b,c,e}, and N(e)={c,d}. The ordering (a,b,c,d,e) has later graph neighbourhoods {b,c}, {c,d}, {d,e}, {e}, and ∅, all cliques; this certifies that the graph is a chordal graph without enumerating its graph cycles. Its maximal cliques {a,b,c}, {b,c,d}, {c,d,e} form a junction tree in that order, with intersections {b,c} and {c,d}.
To find an ordering, maximum cardinality search starts with all scores zero, repeatedly selects an unselected vertex of largest score, and increases each unselected graph neighbour's score by one. Reverse the selection order to obtain a candidate perfect elimination ordering. For the three-triangle graph, one valid selection sequence is (e,d,c,b,a), with scores at selection 0,1,2,2,2; reversing it gives the displayed deletion order. On a chordal graph every tie choice works. On an arbitrary graph, test the resulting later graph neighbourhoods for the clique condition to recognize chordal graphs. Suitable adjacency lists, score buckets and a linear-time verification method give O(∣V∣+∣E∣) recognition.[ref]
The deletion rule also explains sparse Gaussian elimination. For a symmetric positive-definite matrix whose matrix graph is G, eliminating pivot v applies the Schur complement update
auw​⟵auw​−avv​auv​avw​​.
(5)
Only pairs of remaining graph neighbours of v can acquire new off-diagonal entries. A perfect elimination ordering already has all those edges, so Cholesky decomposition creates no symbolic fill-in. Positive definiteness ensures nonzero pivots in exact arithmetic. Special numerical cancellation can suppress predicted entries, and floating-point rounding affects their values.[ref] In the three-triangle graph, deleting c first instead connects every pair in {a,b,d,e} and adds exactly ad,ae,be. The graph was already a chordal graph; the extra fill-in comes from the ordering.
One further reward is optimal graph coloring. Process a perfect elimination ordering backwards and give each vertex the smallest positive color absent from its already colored graph neighbours. Those graph neighbours form a clique, so this greedy algorithm uses at most the clique number ω(G) colors; any clique of that size requires at least that many. In the three-triangle graph, coloring (e,d,c,b,a) gives colors (1,2,3,1,2), so both the chromatic number and the clique number are three. Every maximal clique also occurs among {vi​}∪Ni+​: take its earliest vertex and use maximality. The same ordering therefore supports graph coloring, maximal clique extraction and sparse computation.
Historically, Donald J. Rose, Robert E. Tarjan and George S. Lueker's 1976 paper connected graph elimination to symmetric sparse matrices and gave a search-based O(∣V∣+∣E∣) algorithm for finding a perfect elimination ordering when one exists. Its abstract distinguishes a minimal elimination ordering from a minimum one: removing avoidable fill-in does not by itself minimize the total number of added edges.[ref]

A simplicial vertex is a graph vertex whose graph neighbourhood is a clique. Every isolated vertex and every leaf of a graph qualifies. In the three-triangle chordal graph, initially a,e qualify, but b only becomes a simplicial vertex after deleting a. This is a property of adjacency in a graph; a vertex of a simplicial complex is an element of a different kind of structure.

Maximum cardinality search

Words: 64
Perfect elimination ordering OurBigBook.com
Maximum cardinality search is a graph search in which an unselected vertex's score counts its already selected graph neighbours. Repeatedly select a vertex of maximum score, breaking ties arbitrarily, and update its unselected graph neighbours. On a chordal graph, the reverse selection order is a perfect elimination ordering. On C4​, selecting (a,b,c,d) instead yields candidate deletion order (d,c,b,a); d's later graph neighbours a,c are not adjacent, so the clique check fails.[ref]

Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The Johnson graph has the k-element subsets of an n-element set as vertices, with two vertices adjacent exactly when their intersection has k−1 elements. Relabelling the ground set gives graph automorphisms. The maximal cliques of a Johnson graph allow reconstruction of those ground-set labels when the two clique sizes are different.

Distance in a Johnson graph (d(A,B)=k−∣A∩B∣)

Words: 65
Johnson graph OurBigBook.com
One edge of a Johnson graph replaces one element of a k-subset, so it can increase intersection with a fixed target by at most one. Replacing each element outside the target by one missing target element gives a path reaching this lower bound. Equal-distance ordered pairs have equal sizes of intersection, the two differences and the remaining ground set; a permutation matching these four regions proves distance transitivity.

Maximal cliques of a Johnson graph (n−k+1andk+1)

Johnson graph OurBigBook.com
For 1<k<n−1, the maximal cliques of J(n,k) are the families containing a fixed (k−1)-subset, of size n−k+1, and the families contained in a fixed (k+1)-subset, of size k+1. To see why these exhaust the possibilities, write two adjacent vertices as D∪{a} and D∪{b}. A common adjacent vertex either contains D or lies in D∪{a,b}. A vertex of the first kind outside that union is not adjacent to a vertex of the second kind omitting an element of D, so a clique cannot mix these alternatives. For J(n,3) and n≥5, n=6, the clique sizes n−2 and four distinguish the families containing pairs. Their incidence recovers J(n,2), whose stars of size n−1 distinguish the individual ground-set points from its triangular cliques.

Shortest path problem (minp:s⇝t​∑e∈p​we​)

Words: 2k Articles: 8
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The shortest path problem asks for a graph path from a source vertex s to a destination vertex t minimizing its total edge weight. Here we​ is the cost of traversing edge e, and costs add along the graph path. If no route exists, its shortest-path distance is ∞. With nonnegative edge weights, deleting cycles in a graph from a walk never increases its cost, so repetitions cannot improve the optimum.
Consider the undirected graph with vertex set V={A,B,C,D} and the six edge weights
wAB​=4,wAC​=1,wCB​=2,wBD​=1,wCD​=5,wAD​=10.
(6)
Each edge can be traversed in either direction at the same cost. The direct graph path A,D costs 10; A,B,D costs 4+1=5; A,C,D costs 1+5=6. The cheapest graph path is A,C,B,D, costing 1+2+1=4. The remaining graph path A,B,C,D costs 11, exhausting the possibilities without repeated vertices.
Thus fewest edges and least total cost are different objectives. Breadth-first search minimizes the number of edges, which suffices when every edge has the same positive cost. Unequal nonnegative costs call for the Dijkstra algorithm. On a map, weights might be minutes rather than kilometres: a longer-looking route can arrive sooner. This is why a weighted graph separates the network's connections from what a particular journey costs.

Label-setting shortest-path algorithm

Words: 62
Shortest path problem OurBigBook.com
An algorithm that makes each vertex's distance permanent once it is selected. With nonnegative directed edge lengths, the Dijkstra algorithm selects the unfinalized vertex with least tentative distance; a shorter route through another unfinalized vertex is impossible because its remaining route has at least that next tentative distance. For an all-to-one problem, incoming directed edges to the selected vertex are relaxed. Negative lengths can invalidate this finalization argument.

Bellman inequalities (di​≤cij​+dj​)

Words: 517
Shortest path problem OurBigBook.com
The Bellman inequalities turn local directed edge checks into a global certificate for the shortest path problem. Here the convention is all-to-one: every journey ends at a fixed vertex r, and cij​ is the cost of the original directed edge i→j. Work in a finite directed graph with finite real costs. Write Li​ for candidate labels, normalized by Lr​=0, on the vertices that can reach r. A feasible potential means precisely that these finite labels satisfy
Li​≤cij​+Lj​
(7)
for every directed edge within that set. These labels give lower bounds on costs to r. A discovered directed path of cost Ui​ instead gives an upper bound. The following constructed graph shows both bounds and the exact distances between them; its weights are illustrative costs, not measured travel data.
The arrows in the picture point toward the destination, whereas edge relaxation propagates an improved label in the opposite direction: an improved dj​ can lower di​. In the pictured graph, the directed paths from a to r cost 7, 2+3=5, and 2−2+4=4. Thus δ(a,r)=4. The candidate L=(3,1,3,0) in vertex order (a,b,c,r) is feasible, but underestimates the exact distances (4,2,4,0). Merely satisfying the Bellman inequalities does not make a candidate exact.
Why do they give lower bounds? Along any directed path i=v0​→v1​→⋯→vk​=r, successive substitution gives
Li​≤∑ℓ=0k−1​cvℓ​vℓ+1​​+Lr​=∑ℓ=0k−1​cvℓ​vℓ+1​​.
(8)
The same calculation works for a directed walk, with repeated vertices allowed. Taking the infimum of route costs gives Li​≤δ(i,r). A discovered route gives δ(i,r)≤Ui​. If the bounds meet, Li​=Ui​, they certify an optimum without enumerating routes. Equivalently, check the Bellman inequalities for the proposed distances and exhibit directed paths realizing them. The authored Bellman-Ford algorithm implementation checks the corresponding single-source inequalities and equality on recorded route edges; reversing every directed edge gives this all-to-one convention.[ref]
For the exact labels in the picture, the slack cij​+dj​−di​ is respectively 0,3,1,0,0 on a→b, a→r, b→r, b→c, c→r. Zero slack means equality; the zero-slack directed path a→b→c→r realizes the cost 4. This is the useful beauty of the certificate: a few local inequalities rule out every cheaper journey, while one explicit journey attains the bound.
Keep unreachable vertices separate: δ(i,r)=∞ when no directed path to r exists, and a finite lower bound alone cannot certify that fact. Extended labels can use ∞+c=∞ for finite c, but never compute a slack as ∞−∞. If i can reach a negative-cost directed cycle and then reach r, repeatedly traversing the directed cycle makes route costs unbounded below: their infimum is −∞, with no finite shortest directed walk. A finite feasible potential on such a directed cycle is impossible, since summing its Bellman inequalities would give 0≤∑cij​<0. A negative-cost directed cycle that cannot reach r does not affect distances to r. These are statements about unrestricted directed walks; requiring a directed path with no repeated vertices is a different optimization problem when negative-cost directed cycles exist.[ref]
For the single-source convention, the same original directed edge u→v instead gives L(v)≤L(u)+wuv​ with L(s)=0, a lower bound on distance from s. The endpoint carrying the label on the left therefore changes with the direction of the problem.

Label-correcting shortest-path algorithm

Words: 52
Shortest path problem OurBigBook.com
An algorithm whose tentative distance labels may be revised repeatedly until all relevant Bellman inequalities hold. Bellman-Ford algorithm uses this approach: a label is an upper bound supplied by a discovered directed path, and relaxing an directed edge can replace it with a shorter discovered directed path. A finite label is not declared permanent merely because it has been processed.

Bellman-Ford algorithm

Words: 71
Shortest path problem OurBigBook.com
For an all-to-one shortest path problem with root r, initialize dr(0)​=0 and all other labels to infinity. Set di(k)​=min(di(k−1)​,min(i,j)∈A​{cij​+dj(k−1)​}), keeping the root at zero. Induction identifies the labels with the shortest directed paths using at most k directed edges. Without a reachable negative directed cycle, ∣V∣−1 rounds suffice after removing directed cycles from a shortest walk. In-place or queue variants repeatedly relax incoming directed edges to an improved label. Labels may decrease multiple times, so this is a label-correcting shortest-path algorithm.

Dijkstra algorithm (d(v)=dist(s,v))

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Shortest path problem OurBigBook.com
The Dijkstra algorithm solves the single-source shortest path problem in a finite graph with nonnegative edge weights, finding distances to all reachable vertices. Start with tentative distance d(A)=0 and d(v)=∞ elsewhere. Repeatedly choose the unfinalized vertex with least tentative distance, declare that label permanent, and perform edge relaxation on its outgoing edges. For an undirected graph, inspect both directions. A finite tentative distance always records the cost of a discovered graph path, but can improve before finalization.
In our example, finalizing A discovers C at 1, B at 4, and D at 10. Choose C next: edge relaxation through C lowers B to 1+2=3 and D to 1+5=6. Choose B: edge relaxation through B lowers D to 3+1=4. Finally choose D. The permanent distances are therefore A:0, C:1, B:3, D:4; the evolving tentative distances were B:4→3 and D:10→6→4.

A0None: source1

Following shortest-path predecessors backwards gives D,B,C,A; reversing the order gives A,C,B,D. If only this destination matters, stop when D is finalized. Stopping when D is first discovered would incorrectly return 10. If the smallest remaining tentative distance is ∞, all remaining vertices are unreachable.
Why is the permanent choice safe? Suppose the selected vertex u had a cheaper graph path. Let y be the first unfinalized vertex on that graph path. Its preceding vertex was finalized, so edge relaxation has already offered y a label no larger than that prefix's cost. Nonnegative remaining edge weights make the whole cost at least this prefix's cost; selection gives d(u)≤d(y). A cheaper graph path would contradict these comparisons. Zero weights are allowed; ties can be resolved arbitrarily. This is the reason the label-setting shortest-path algorithm works, rather than a lucky feature of the drawing.
Negative weights break that reasoning. In a directed graph with s→u costing 2, s→v costing 5, and v→u costing −4, the Dijkstra algorithm would finalize u at 2 before discovering the cheaper cost 1. The Bellman-Ford algorithm handles negative edge weights when no relevant negative directed cycle exists.
With an adjacency list and an indexed binary heap implementing a priority queue, the time complexity is O((∣V∣+∣E∣)log∣V∣) for ∣V∣≥2, using Big O notation. Each vertex is extracted at most once, each edge is inspected once per direction, and each successful edge relaxation decreases a heap key in O(log∣V∣) time. This assumes constant-cost arithmetic and comparisons; exact computation with very large weights adds their representation cost. The queue uses O(∣V∣) space beyond the graph. Simply scanning all remaining vertices gives O(∣V∣2+∣E∣) instead.[ref][ref]
The 1959 paper presents the shortest path problem as its second problem, after the minimum spanning tree problem, and grows known shortest routes in increasing distance order.[ref] In his later recollection, Dijkstra dated the shortest-route discovery to 1956: a demonstration for the ARMAC computer used a simplified Dutch railway map and printed the route between towns. A practical request became an enduring algorithm because the same distance rule applies to any suitable graph.[ref]

These are different failure models. [ref]

Thus A is the only cut vertex. Every edge lies on a triangle in a graph, so deleting any single edge still leaves a graph path between its endpoints along the other two edges. There are no bridges in a graph.

For a disconnected example, adjoin an isolated vertex Z to the first graph. Now k(G)=2, deleting A gives k(G−A)=3, and deleting Z gives k(G−Z)=1. The original graph was already disconnected, but A is still a cut vertex; Z is not. The empty graph has count zero, so deleting the only vertex of a one-vertex graph does not create a cut vertex. Nor is either endpoint of a single isolated edge a cut vertex, although that edge is a bridge in a graph.
In a communications network, a cut vertex models a router whose failure separates surviving routers. The shared-A example shows why having an alternative graph path around each individual edge does not protect against failure of the common router. An additional edge from B to D removes this particular vulnerability: after deleting A, B,D still join the two sides. A bridge in a graph instead models a vulnerable link. This distinction tells us whether to add another cable between existing devices or a route avoiding an indispensable device; it describes connectivity, rather than traffic capacity or failure probabilities.
The beautiful structural consequence is that a graph splits into biconnected components joined at cut vertices. Within each nontrivial robust piece, a single vertex failure cannot separate the other vertices; between pieces, the shared cut vertices reveal the bottlenecks. Also, a Hamiltonian graph has no cut vertex: deleting any vertex from its Hamilton cycle leaves a Hamiltonian path through all remaining vertices.
Historically, Tarjan's June 1972 paper developed depth-first search as a tool for finding biconnected components in time linear in the numbers of vertices and edges. [ref] In his 1983 recollection, Tarjan credited Hopcroft with the original linear-time biconnected component algorithm during their collaboration beginning in summer 1970, and described the published version as a refinement. The historical lesson is how a carefully organized traversal turns many separate deletion experiments into one computation. [ref]

Biconnected component

Words: 104

A biconnected component is a maximal connected subgraph with no cut vertex of its own. We use the block convention that also includes each bridge in a graph with its two endpoint vertices, and each isolated vertex, as a biconnected component. A biconnected component with at least three vertices stays connected after any single vertex deletion. Distinct biconnected components share at most one vertex; the vertices belonging to more than one biconnected component are exactly the cut vertices. The shared-A example has two biconnected components, its two triangles in a graph. The joined-CD example has three: ABC, the bridge in a graph CD with its endpoints, and DEF. The edges partition into these pieces, while the shared cut vertices occur in several pieces. [ref]

The DFS discovery time of a vertex is its first-visit number in depth-first search, assigned by an increasing counter. Discovery edges form a rooted tree in each connected component of a graph. For the joined-CD example, starting at A and visiting graph neighbours in lexicographic order gives first visits A,B,C,D,E,F, numbered 1,2,3,4,5,6; its discovery edges are AB,BC,CD,DE,EF. These numbers encode the chosen traversal, not an invariant of the graph.

DFS lowpoint (low(v))

Words: 445
Cut vertex OurBigBook.com
For a finite simple graph that is an undirected graph, the DFS lowpoint of v is the smallest DFS discovery time reachable by following zero or more discovery edges down its rooted tree, then at most one non-discovery edge to an ancestor. Staying at v is allowed. Ignore the reverse traversal of the discovery edge to the parent in a rooted tree: it is the same edge, not an escape route. Start with low(v)=disc(v). On returning from a child in a rooted tree w, replace low(v) by min{low(v),low(w)}. For a non-discovery edge from v to an earlier ancestor a, replace it by min{low(v),disc(a)}. This summarizes how far upward the explored branch can reconnect. [ref]
The cut vertex criterion has a separate case for each root of a tree in the discovery forest:
  • A nonroot vertex u is a cut vertex exactly when some child in a rooted tree w satisfies low(w)≥disc(u).
  • A root of a tree is a cut vertex exactly when it has at least two children in a rooted tree, counting discovery edges, rather than all graph neighbours.
  • A discovery edge uw is a bridge in a graph exactly when low(w)>disc(u). A non-discovery edge is never a bridge in a graph.
Why does equality matter? If low(w)=disc(u), the branch below w can reconnect to u, so the discovery edge uw lies on a graph cycle and is not a bridge in a graph. Deleting the vertex u destroys that reconnection too. If u has a parent in a rooted tree, the branch is then separated from that parent in a rooted tree, explaining the non-strict cut vertex test. For a root of a tree, there is no earlier side to separate from; distinct discovery branches cannot have an edge between them, since depth-first search would have explored them as one branch. This gives the two-children in a rooted tree rule. These are proof outlines of the criteria. [ref][ref]
In the joined-CD example with DFS discovery times 1,2,3,4,5,6, the DFS lowpoints in label order are 1,1,1,4,4,4. For C and its child in a rooted tree D, 4>3: CD is a bridge in a graph, and C is a cut vertex. For D and its child in a rooted tree E, 4=4: D is a cut vertex, although DE is not a bridge in a graph. The root of a tree A has only one child in a rooted tree, B, so it is not a cut vertex. In the shared-A example, the root of a tree A has two children in a rooted tree, B and D, and is a cut vertex, while every DFS lowpoint is 1 and no edge passes the strict bridge in a graph test.
Restart depth-first search at every undiscovered vertex to cover a disconnected graph, applying the root of a tree rule separately in each connected component of a graph. With adjacency lists and constant-cost label operations, computing all DFS lowpoints, cut vertices and bridges in a graph has time complexity O(∣V∣+∣E∣) in Big O notation, because each vertex is discovered once and each edge is inspected twice. The simple parent-skipping rule assumes a simple graph. In a multigraph, skip only the actual parent edge, identified individually: a parallel edge to the same parent in a rooted tree is a valid reconnection and can prevent the first edge from being a bridge in a graph. The criteria here concern undirected graphs; a directed graph requires a different connectivity analysis.

A walk records a journey through a graph as a finite alternating sequence
W=(v0​,e1​,v1​,…,em​,vm​),m≥0,
(12)
where each edge ei​ joins the consecutive vertices vi−1​ and vi​. Both vertices and edges may repeat. Its length is m, counting edge traversals with repetitions, rather than counting different edges or measuring the drawing. Here a graph path means a walk with no repeated vertices; a trail instead forbids repeated edges. These conventions distinguish a journey's record from the subgraph consisting of the connections it used.[ref]
Unless stated otherwise, the examples below use a finite simple graph that is an undirected graph, so an edge may be traversed in either direction. In a multigraph, retain each edge's individual identity as well as its endpoint vertices: two parallel edges are different choices for the same step. If self-loops are allowed, traversing one leaves the current vertex unchanged but adds one to the length. In a directed graph, each step must follow its directed edge from its initial to its terminal vertex, giving a directed walk; reversing a journey need not be possible.[ref]
We allow the zero-length walk (v) at every vertex v. It uses no edges, so it is also a trail and a graph path, and its coinciding endpoints make it a closed walk. This means staying put is a legitimate journey; a graph with no vertices has no such walk. Positive-length restrictions will be stated explicitly.[ref]
Use the same constructed graph throughout these three sections:
V={A,B,C,D,E,F},E={AB,BC,CA,AD,DE,EA,AF}.
(13)
Here AB denotes the unordered pair {A,B}, and CA=AC. Two triangles in a graph, ABC and ADE, share A, with one extra edge AF. These are schematic connections, not measured roads; the highlighted connections in the diagram show which edges are used, while the numbered sequence records their order.
The length-six walk B,C,A,B,C,A,F uses BC and CA twice, so it is not a trail. The length-six trail B,C,A,D,E,A,F returns to A but uses six different edges, so it is not a graph path. The length-three graph path B,C,A,F repeats neither vertices nor edges. Thus
{graph paths}⊊{trails}⊊{walks}
(14)
for this particular graph. The restrictions answer different routing questions: revisiting a junction is harmless for many journeys, whereas reusing a serviced road segment can matter for an inspection route. Travel costs require a weighted graph; a walk's cost adds the weight of each traversal, even when an edge is used again.
Every finite walk from s to t contains a graph path from s to t after deleting detours. For a proof outline, if vi​=vj​ with i<j, delete the intervening closed walk. The retained steps still meet at the same vertex, and the length strictly decreases. Repeating terminates with no repeated vertices, or with the zero-length graph path when s=t. This explains why reachability can be formulated using either walks or graph paths. With nonnegative edge weights, deletion also cannot increase cost, connecting the argument to the shortest path problem; with negative weights that cost conclusion fails.[ref]

Trail in a graph

Words: 269
Walk in a graph OurBigBook.com
A trail is a walk whose edge sequence e1​,…,em​ has no repetitions. Its vertices may repeat, including its first and last vertices. The zero-length walk is a trail because it repeats no edge. Every graph path is a trail, but the converse fails: the trail in the shared example is
B,BC,C,CA,A,AD,D,DE,E,EA,A,AF,F.
(15)
Its six edges BC,CA,AD,DE,EA,AF are pairwise distinct, although A occurs twice. Visiting a junction again and traversing a road segment again are different events.[ref]
In an undirected graph, traversing AB and then BA repeats the same edge; direction of travel does not give it a new identity. In a multigraph with distinct parallel edges p,q joining X and Y, the closed walk (X,p,Y,q,X) is a trail, whereas (X,p,Y,p,X) is not. Both have the same vertex sequence X,Y,X. In a directed graph, separate directed edges X→Y and Y→X may instead be used once each; record their identities and obey their directions. Thus testing a trail means checking the actual edge records, not merely checking consecutive endpoint labels.
For a finite graph, a trail has length at most ∣E∣; unrestricted walks can have arbitrarily large length whenever a positive-length closed walk exists, since it can be repeated. An Eulerian trail is the special trail that uses every edge, so its length is exactly ∣E∣. Our length-six trail omits AB and is therefore not an Eulerian trail. In a road-inspection model, a trail describes servicing its selected segments once while allowing returns to junctions; requiring service of every segment leads to the Eulerian trail question. If extra travel between serviced segments is necessary, the complete journey can be a walk even when each segment is serviced only once. This distinction keeps the service requirement separate from the route actually travelled.

Closed walk (vm​=v0​)

Words: 519
Walk in a graph OurBigBook.com
A closed walk is a walk with equal endpoint vertices, vm​=v0​. Under our convention this includes the zero-length walk (v); returning after traversing at least one edge requires m>0. Closure imposes no other restriction on repeated vertices or edges. In a directed graph, a closed directed walk must also follow every directed edge in its permitted direction.[ref]
In the shared simple graph, A,F,A is a length-two closed walk that immediately backtracks along AF. It is not a trail, since AF is used twice, and it is not a graph cycle. The length-six closed walk A,B,C,A,D,E,A is a trail, since its six edges are distinct, but is not a graph cycle: it returns to A midway through the journey. The length-three closed walk A,B,C,A is a graph cycle, with all vertices distinct apart from the required endpoint repetition. In a simple graph that is an undirected graph, a graph cycle has length at least three; the two-step backtrack is excluded.[ref]
A positive-length closed walk therefore need not reveal a graph cycle: even a tree permits an out-and-back journey on an edge. A positive-length closed trail in a simple graph does contain a graph cycle. For a proof outline, choose a shortest positive-length consecutive portion of the trail whose endpoint vertices coincide. It cannot repeat an internal vertex, since that would give a shorter such portion; it cannot have length one or two because self-loops and repeated edges are excluded. It is consequently a graph cycle. Cutting it out leaves another closed trail, possibly of length zero, so repetition partitions the original edges into graph cycles. In our six-step example these are the two triangles in a graph. A closed trail using every edge would be an Euler circuit; here AF is omitted.
Counting return journeys makes closed walks useful even when they repeat edges. For a finite simple graph with adjacency matrix M, the walk count from powers of an adjacency matrix gives (Mk)uv​ length-k walks from u to v, for every nonnegative integer k. A proof outline is that matrix multiplication appends one allowed step, summing over the previous endpoint; M0 is the identity matrix, recording the unique zero-length walk at each vertex. Consequently
(Mk)vv​=#{length-k closed walks starting at v},tr(Mk)=∑v∈V​(Mk)vv​.

A closed walk naturally models a delivery or inspection journey that returns to its depot. Repeated vertices let it combine several excursions; repeated edges let it serve a dead end and return. That argument assumes direct travel between the retained locations is permitted, as in a complete graph weighted by Euclidean distance; an arbitrary road network need not contain those shortcut edges.

Graph minor (H≼G)

Words: 2k Articles: 7
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A graph minor compresses connected regions of a graph into single vertices while retaining selected connections between them. For finite simple graphs, H≼G means that some sequence of deleting vertices, deleting edges, and performing edge contractions produces H up to graph isomorphism. Deleting a vertex also deletes all its incident edges; deleting an edge leaves its endpoints. The edge contraction convention here removes resulting self-loops and duplicate edges.[ref]
For an exact small example, let G be the cycle graph C4​ with vertices u,v,a,b and edges uv,va,ab,bu. Contract uv to a new vertex w. The surviving edges are wa,ab,bw, giving the complete graph K3​. Thus K3​≼C4​, although C4​ has no triangle in a graph as a subgraph. The branch sets of a graph minor are {u,v},{a},{b}, with the original edges va,ab,bu witnessing all three required adjacencies. The first panel of the edge contraction diagram shows this operation.
A subgraph uses existing vertices and edges; a topological minor permits a graph subdivision of the target as a subgraph, so target edges become graph paths with mutually disjoint interiors and no target vertex in an interior. An ordinary graph minor permits whole connected branch sets of a graph minor in place of target vertices. Every topological minor is a graph minor, by contracting the replacement graph paths.[ref]
The converse fails. Take the tree with edges uv,ua,ub,vc,vd. Contracting uv gives the star graph K1,4​. Yet the original tree has maximum degree three, whereas every graph subdivision of K1,4​ retains a centre of degree of a vertex four. Hence K1,4​ is a graph minor but not a topological minor of this tree. The difference is that a connected branch set of a graph minor may gather connections incident to several original vertices.
The counts of vertices and edges never increase under these operations. However, the C4​ example shows that being a bipartite graph is not preserved: its graph minor K3​ contains an odd cycle. Its chromatic number also increases from two to three. A connected graph stays connected under an edge contraction, because the image of each graph path still connects its endpoints, but deletion can disconnect it. Thus one must check the particular graph property before treating it as preserved by taking graph minors.
Being a planar graph is preserved: in a crossing-free drawing, shrink a contracted edge and bring its incident edges into the merged vertex; deletion merely removes parts of the drawing. This makes a nonplanar graph minor a certificate that the original graph is nonplanar. More strongly, for a finite simple graph, being a planar graph is equivalent to having neither the complete graph K5​ nor the complete bipartite graph K3,3​ as a graph minor. Finding the corresponding branch sets of a graph minor settles nonplanarity even when no literal K5​ or K3,3​ subgraph is present. The converse is a substantial theorem, rather than a consequence of preservation alone.[ref]

Topological minor (H≼top​G)

Words: 427
Graph minor OurBigBook.com
A topological minor records a network pattern whose vertices remain individual junctions but whose edges may become longer routes. For finite simple graphs, H≼top​G means that G contains a subgraph that is a graph subdivision of H up to graph isomorphism. Equivalently, choose distinct branch vertices of a graph subdivision bv​∈V(G) for v∈V(H) and a graph path Puv​ from bu​ to bv​ for every uv∈E(H). These are internally vertex-disjoint paths, and no internal vertex of any Puv​ is a branch vertex of a graph subdivision. Only endpoints corresponding to a shared target vertex may be shared.[ref]
The graph subdivision example below replaces two edges of a triangle in a graph by routes of two and three edges while retaining its attached leaf of a graph. If the host graph also contains an extra edge BD, the same routes still witness a topological minor: delete BD when selecting the subgraph. An induced subgraph is not required. However, routes that merely connect the right pairs are insufficient: using a branch vertex of a graph subdivision as an intermediate junction, or making two routes share an internal vertex, can change the local network structure.
Every topological minor is a graph minor. In each branch path of a graph subdivision, contract all but one edge; the disjoint interiors let this shorten each route without merging distinct branch vertices of a graph subdivision. This recovers H after deleting unused vertices and edges.[ref] The converse fails because an ordinary branch set of a graph minor can gather several junctions into one.
For the tree T with vertices u,v,a,b,c,d and edges uv,ua,ub,vc,vd, contracting uv produces a star graph K1,4​: the branch sets of a graph minor are {u,v},{a},{b},{c},{d}. Both u,v have degree of a vertex three; each of the other four vertices is a leaf of a graph with degree of a vertex one. The new centre w has four distinct graph neighbours a,b,c,d; its degree of a vertex is 3+3−2=4, in agreement with the edge contraction formula.
Yet K1,4​ is not a topological minor of T. In a graph subdivision of K1,4​, four branch paths of a graph subdivision must leave the centre through four different edges; sharing their first internal vertex would violate internal disjointness. Thus any host needs a vertex of degree of a vertex at least four, whereas Δ(T)=3. More generally, H≼top​G implies Δ(H)≤Δ(G), where Δ is the maximum degree of a graph. This bound concerns the host graph; extra unused edges may make its branch vertices of a graph subdivision have larger degrees of vertices than their target counterparts.
This distinction matters when a network's individual junctions have a limited number of connections: replacing a connection by a route preserves the number of routes meeting at each chosen junction, while contracting a connected region can combine connections from separate junctions. It also explains why a small nonplanar pattern can hide inside long routes. By Kuratowski's theorem, a finite simple graph is a planar graph exactly when it has neither the complete graph K5​ nor the complete bipartite graph K3,3​ as a topological minor. The obstruction is a graph subdivision inside the network, regardless of the number of intermediate vertices.

Assume also that no rooted separation of a graph of order below q avoids d+1 of these sets. Then there are m=h−q/2 disjoint connected vertex sets D1​,…,Dm​ such that xi​∈Di​ for 1≤i≤q and each of these first q sets is adjacent to all but at most d of Dq+1​,…,Dm​.

We prove the reduction by induction, first on the vertex count and then on the edge count; any counterexample chosen minimal in this ordering will be impossible.
We may delete edges joining two vertices of S. They cannot affect rooted separations of a graph, since S lies wholly on the first side. Within a branch set, their deletion can only split a graph component into graph components each containing an endpoint in S, so the branch-set hypothesis also persists. An isolated vertex outside S and all branch sets can be deleted. An isolated vertex v∈S is also impossible, since (S,V(G)∖{v}) has order q−1 and avoids at least h−q≥d+q/2≥d+1 sets. Thus in a minimal counterexample S is independent, and every isolated vertex outside S belongs to a singleton branch set.
Consider a rooted separation of a graph (A,B) of order exactly q avoiding at least d+1 branch sets, and put S′=A∩B. Restrict to G′=G[B]−E(G[S′]) and Ci′​=Ci​∩B. Each Ci′​ is nonempty: any Ci​ not itself avoided is adjacent to at least one of the d+1 avoided sets, and the endpoint of such an edge in Ci​ must lie in B. If a graph component of G′[Ci′​] misses S′, it lies in B∖A and is a whole graph component of G[Ci​], with no vertex of S. The original hypothesis then forces G[Ci​] to be connected and Ci′​=Ci​, entirely outside A. Thus each restricted set is connected or all its graph components meet S′. In particular every Cj′​ missing S′ equals an original set outside A, so all its required adjacencies from Ci′​ persist.
A rooted separation of a graph (A′,B′) of G′ avoiding d+1 restricted sets lifts to (A∪A′,B′) in G, of the same order: an avoided restricted set misses S′, hence is an original set outside A. The edges removed inside S′ do not obstruct lifting, since S′⊆A′. This proves the required separation hypothesis for G′. If G′ is smaller, induction gives the desired connected sets rooted at S′. Moreover G[A] has q disjoint graph paths from S to S′, by the Menger theorem. Indeed a separator of smaller order between these sets would give a rooted separation of a graph of G of smaller order still avoiding those d+1 original sets. Truncate the graph paths at their first visits to S′, label their endpoints accordingly, and adjoin each graph path to the corresponding rooted connected set. They meet B only in their distinct endpoints, so this gives the desired sets for G, a contradiction. Consequently in a minimal counterexample every such separation of order q has B=V(G) and A=S, an independent set.
Now contract any edge whose endpoints do not belong to two different branch sets. Its endpoints cannot both lie in S, so the image of S still has size q. The branch-set conditions persist. If the contraction created a forbidden rooted separation of a graph of order below q, its lift would have order below q, except possibly when the contracted vertex lies in its separator. In that case the lifted order increases by one and is at most q. Equality would put the contracted edge inside A, contradicting the just-proved independence of A for an order-q separation avoiding d+1 sets. Thus the separation hypothesis also persists. Applying induction in the contracted graph and expanding the contracted vertex would produce the required disjoint connected sets. Hence every edge in a minimal counterexample joins two different branch sets.
Every vertex outside the branch sets would be isolated, since every edge joins two branch sets; such an isolated vertex could be deleted. Thus the branch sets cover the graph. Each nonsingleton branch set is therefore an independent set, and all its vertices belong to S, because each of its singleton graph components must meet S. ∣V(G)∣−q−∣Y∣≥∣V(G)∣−q−c+1≥h−2c​−q+1≥h−23q​+1≥d+1.

unused vertices, all singleton original branch sets. Choose m−q of them for the remaining Di​. To turn a model into an operation sequence, keep a spanning tree inside each G[Bx​], keep one witnessing edge for each edge of H, and delete all other edges and unused vertices. Contract each chosen spanning tree to one vertex. Disjointness prevents two target vertices from merging; connectedness provides the edge contractions that merge each individual region. Conversely, track the original vertices merged into every surviving vertex during a deletion-and-edge contraction sequence. They form disjoint connected branch sets of a graph minor, and each surviving edge comes from an original edge between its two regions. A list of these regions, their connecting trees, and their witnessing edges therefore gives a directly checkable certificate.

A vertex cover chooses vertices that collectively touch every edge of a graph. Think of placing monitors at junctions: if a monitor watches every connection incident to its junction, a vertex cover watches all connections. The minimum vertex cover asks how few monitors suffice. This is a model of covering connections through their endpoints, rather than of monitoring distances in the drawing.
For a finite simple graph G=(V,E), a vertex cover is a subset C⊆V satisfying
{u,v}∈E⟹u∈C or v∈C.
(25)
Both endpoints may be selected; the condition requires at least one. An isolated vertex covers no edge, so a minimum vertex cover never needs it.[ref]
Take the cycle graph C5​ with vertices 0,1,2,3,4 and edges 01,12,23,34,40. The set C={1,3,4} is a vertex cover: vertex 1 covers 01 and 12, vertex 3 covers 23 and 34, and vertex 4 covers 40 as well as 34. In particular, the closing edge 40 is covered even though vertex 0 is unselected.
The unselected vertices I=V∖C={0,2} form an independent set. This is the key connection: an edge missed by C would have both endpoints in I, precisely what an independent set forbids. For every subset C⊆V,
C is a vertex cover⟺V∖C is an independent set.
(26)
Here V∖C is the complement of a set within V; the graph itself keeps all its edges. The complement graph is a different construction.[ref]
The endpoints of any maximal matching form a vertex cover: an edge avoiding all endpoints would enlarge that matching in a graph. Consequently a graph with no matching in a graph of size s has a vertex cover of size at most 2(s−1). This supplies a convenient vertex cover, but it need not be a minimum vertex cover.

Graph coloring

Words: 4k Articles: 44
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A graph coloring assigns labels called colours to elements of a graph, subject to specified constraints. Here we focus on proper vertex colouring of a simple graph G=(V,E): it is an undirected graph with a finite set of vertices, and a colouring with at most k colours is a function
c:V→{1,…,k},{u,v}∈E⟹c(u)=c(v).
(35)
The colour labels need not be visual colours: they can represent time slots or resources. Unused labels are allowed. Properness concerns graph adjacency, so moving vertices in a drawing does not change whether the graph coloring is valid.[ref]
Each colour class c−1(i) is an independent set: no edge has both endpoints in it. Conversely, a set partition of V into independent sets gives a proper graph coloring by assigning one colour to each part. Thus graph coloring groups mutually compatible objects, and its chromatic number asks for the fewest such groups.
For an illustrative scheduling model, let each vertex represent an activity of equal duration and each edge represent a pair that cannot occur in the same time slot. A proper graph coloring is then a schedule respecting those pairwise conflicts. If the conflicts form a cycle graph C4​ with edges 12,23,34,41, activities 1,3 can share one slot and 2,4 another. This model assumes interchangeable slots and includes only the pairwise conflicts encoded by the graph.[ref]
The word "colouring" also occurs in edge coloring, which requires different colours on edges sharing an endpoint. The chromatic number discussed here always refers to proper vertex colouring.

A proper vertex coloring assigns labels to the vertices of a graph so that vertices joined by an edge have different labels. Each colour class is an independent set. The chromatic number is the least number of labels needed for this form of graph coloring.

Maintain lists of available colours, tentatively colour small random portions, erase conflicts and prune colours used by neighbours. In a triangle-free graph, a vertex's neighbours form an independent set, which enables local estimates. Track list size and average remaining neighbour congestion per colour; prune unusually congested colours before the next round. Concentration and the Lovász local lemma preserve these invariants until lists have enough slack for completion. Tracking averages matters because triangle-free graphs can still contain many four-cycles and need not have uniform per-colour congestion.

Graph coloring OurBigBook.com
If each neighbourhood misses a fixed positive fraction of the possible pairs at a large degree bound, randomly assign about half that many colours and erase vertices with monochromatic incident edges. A nonadjacent neighbour pair can share a retained colour, giving a neighbour-colour saving. Write the number of successful repeated colours as a difference of two certifiable functions: colours with a nonadjacent pair, minus those for which a neighbour loses that colour. Both change by at most two under one-coordinate changes and have constant-size certificates. Talagrand's convex distance inequality and the Lovász local lemma make their linear expected saving simultaneous at all high-degree vertices; low-degree vertices have slack already. This yields a colouring using a fixed positive fraction fewer than the degree bound.

Greedy coloring

Words: 392 Articles: 2
Graph coloring OurBigBook.com
For a finite simple graph, choose an order of its vertices and process them one at a time. Give each vertex the smallest positive colour label not already used by its coloured neighbours, and keep all earlier assignments. This is greedy coloring: each step makes a locally available choice. The resulting graph coloring is proper because, for each edge, its later endpoint avoids the colour of its earlier endpoint.[ref]
If the maximum degree of a graph is Δ(G), a vertex has at most Δ(G) previously coloured neighbours, forbidding at most that many distinct colours. At least one label among 1,…,Δ(G)+1 remains available. Consequently every order gives
χ(G)≤number of colours used by greedy colouring≤Δ(G)+1.
(36)
This is an upper bound, not a promise that greedy coloring attains the chromatic number.[ref]
Consider the path graph P4​ with edges 12,23,34. In the order 1,2,3,4, greedy coloring assigns the colours 1,2,1,2 respectively. In the order 1,4,2,3, it assigns colours 1,1,2,3 in processing order: vertices 1,4 both get colour 1, then vertex 2 gets colour 2, and finally vertex 3 sees colours 2 and 1 at its two neighbours and must take colour 3. Written in vertex order 1,2,3,4, this second colouring is 1,2,3,1.
The path graph has chromatic number two: the first assignment achieves two colours, and any edge rules out one. Its maximum degree of a graph is two, so three colours in the second assignment still satisfy the bound. The extra colour comes entirely from the processing order. The crown graph gives a larger family where a poor order can make greedy coloring use arbitrarily many colours although the chromatic number remains two.

When t has colour T and the inputs x,y,z have colours in {T,F}, this graph admits an extension to a graph colouring with three colours exactly when at least one input is T. All-false inputs force a=d=F, contradicting their edge. Conversely, use (a,b,c,d,e)=(T,F,B,F,B) if x=T, (T,B,F,F,B) if x=F,y=T, and (F,T,B,B,F) if x=y=F,z=T. The extension property is necessary for both directions of a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

An edge colouring assigns a label called a colour to every edge of a graph: it is a function c:E(G)→{1,…,k}. Here this definition allows arbitrary assignments. Two edges sharing a vertex may receive the same colour. A proper edge colouring imposes the additional condition that such edges receive different colours. Some textbooks use "edge colouring" as shorthand for this proper version; check the convention before applying a theorem.[ref]
The distinction matters in Ramsey theory. In a red-blue edge colouring of a complete graph, a triangle in a graph is monochromatic when its three edges have the same colour. These are arbitrary edge colourings: forbidding equal colours on edges sharing a vertex would forbid the very monochromatic triangles in a graph being sought. For example, assigning red to every edge of K3​ is a valid arbitrary edge colouring, although it is not a proper edge colouring. Colour labels can also stand for time slots: then proper edge colouring turns incompatible jobs into separate rounds.

The line graph makes the relationship with proper vertex colouring explicit: replace each original edge by a vertex, joining two new vertices exactly when their original edges share an endpoint. A proper edge colouring of G becomes a proper vertex colouring of its line graph L(G), so χ′(G)=χ(L(G)). For a multigraph, retain a distinct new vertex for each parallel edge.[ref]
Edge coloring as scheduling
Words: 304
Proper edge coloring OurBigBook.com
Suppose each job occupies two distinct resources for one whole slot, and each resource can serve at most one job in that slot. Make resources vertices and jobs edges. Two jobs conflict exactly when their edges share a vertex, so a valid schedule is a proper edge colouring. Each slot is a matching in a graph; the chromatic index is the minimum number of slots. The colour labels specify the slots, rather than physical colours. This model assumes all jobs are available initially, with equal duration, interchangeable slots and no additional conflicts. The school-timetable motivation in Graph Theory by Reinhard Diestel (author-hosted Colouring preview, opening paragraphs, pp. 123–124) uses this resource-pair interpretation.
Here is a complete example. Two technicians A,B must each use three instruments X,Y,Z once. Each job needs its technician and its instrument simultaneously. The six jobs are the edges of the complete bipartite graph K2,3​:
E={AX,AY,AZ,BX,BY,BZ},M1​={AX,BY},M2​={AY,BZ},M3​={AZ,BX}.
(43)
Within each Mi​, the two jobs use different technicians and different instruments, so Mi​ is a matching in a graph. The three matchings in a graph together cover every job exactly once. Technician A has three jobs, so fewer than three slots cannot suffice; the displayed schedule uses three. This is an optimal proper edge colouring with chromatic index three, witnessed by both a schedule and a resource-workload lower bound.
Repeated jobs requiring the same resource pair become distinct parallel edges of a multigraph, rather than one edge. Additional restrictions change the problem: prescribed allowed slots lead to list edge coloring, while unequal durations, deadlines, or jobs needing more than two resources require a richer scheduling model. Selecting a largest matching in a graph solves a single-round question; a shortest complete schedule must organize all jobs across rounds.

Chromatic index (χ′(G))

Words: 570 Articles: 1
Edge coloring OurBigBook.com
The chromatic index χ′(G), also called the edge chromatic number, is the least number of labels in a proper edge colouring of a finite undirected graph without self-loops. Equivalently, it is the smallest number of matchings in a graph whose set partition covers all the edges. We take χ′(G)=0 when there are no edges. For an arbitrary edge colouring, one colour always suffices whenever an edge exists, so properness is essential to this definition. The chromatic number χ(G) instead colours vertices.[ref]
To establish an exact chromatic index, supply both a proper edge colouring and a reason that fewer colours cannot work. Every edge at a fixed vertex must have its own colour, giving the lower bound χ′(G)≥Δ(G), where Δ(G) is the maximum degree of a graph. The bound need not be attained: it counts a single resource's workload, while conflicts can also accumulate around a graph cycle.
For the triangle in a graph K3​ with edges ab,bc,ca, every pair of edges shares a vertex, so all three require different labels. The assignment c(ab)=1,c(bc)=2,c(ca)=3 works, proving χ′(K3​)=3 although Δ(K3​)=2. In its line graph, those three edges become a three-vertex clique. Treating this as three pair-resource jobs makes the obstruction tangible: each resource has only two jobs, but every pair of jobs conflicts, so no slot can contain two jobs.
For the square cycle graph C4​ with edges ab,bc,cd,da, use c(ab)=c(cd)=1 and c(bc)=c(da)=2. Each colour class is a matching in a graph, and each vertex has one edge of each colour. Since Δ(C4​)=2, this proves χ′(C4​)=2. More generally, alternation closes on any even cycle graph C2m​, m≥2. On an odd cycle C2m+1​, m≥1, two-colour alternation would make the last and first edges share a colour at their common vertex; a third colour on the last edge suffices. Thus even cycle graphs have chromatic index two and odd cycle graphs have chromatic index three. These exact examples show why maximum degree of a graph alone does not determine the answer.

(44)
Here Δ(G) is the maximum degree of a graph, taken as zero when there are no vertices. A bipartite graph has the stronger equality χ′(G)=Δ(G). The six-job complete bipartite graph above attains this lower bound, while the triangle in a graph attains the extra-colour alternative. The simple-graph restriction in the upper bound matters.[ref]
The bipartite graph equality still holds for finite loopless multigraphs, with parallel edges counted separately in each vertex degree. For instance, r parallel jobs between two resources need exactly r slots: every pair conflicts, and Δ=χ′=r. For a general finite loopless multigraph, however, the simple graph upper bound can fail. Put two parallel edges on each side of a triangle in a graph. All six edges pairwise share a vertex, so each needs its own colour; every vertex has degree of a vertex four. Consequently χ′=6>Δ+1=5. A multiplicity-aware bound is χ′(G)≤Δ(G)+μ(G), where μ(G) is the largest number of parallel edges between a pair of vertices. The doubled triangle in a graph has μ=2 and attains that bound. These statements exclude self-loops; the two-distinct-resource scheduling model excludes them too.[ref]
For historical orientation, Graph Theory by Reinhard Diestel (Colouring preview, §5.3, p. 132) dates the bipartite equality to 1916 and Vizing's theorem to 1964. These are textbook attributions; the original papers have not been inspected here. The results state existence of optimal or nearly optimal proper edge colourings, rather than saying that arbitrary greedy choices will find them. The list-chromatic index asks the further question of success for every sufficiently large family of allowed-colour lists.

Chromatic number (χ(G))

Graph coloring OurBigBook.com
For a nonempty finite simple graph G, the chromatic number χ(G) is the least positive integer k for which G has a proper vertex graph coloring with at most k colours. To establish an exact chromatic number, give a colouring using that many colours and explain why fewer cannot suffice. A colouring alone gives only an upper bound.[ref]
These small graphs show why the chromatic number measures more than the presence of triangles in a graph:
  • The cycle graph C3​, also the complete graph K3​, has chromatic number three. Every pair of vertices is adjacent, so three distinct colours are necessary and sufficient.
  • The cycle graph C4​ has chromatic number two. Around the graph cycle, the assignment 1,2,1,2 is proper, and a single colour would violate every edge.
  • The cycle graph C5​ has chromatic number three. With two colours, alternation around the graph cycle would force the first and fifth vertices to have the same colour despite their joining edge. The assignment 1,2,1,2,3 works. Thus a triangle-free graph can still require more than two colours.
  • The complete graph Kn​ has chromatic number n: all n vertices are pairwise adjacent, so each must have its own colour.[ref]
For a cycle graph of even length, alternating two colours closes consistently; for an odd cycle, it does not, and a third colour on the final vertex suffices. More generally, the two-colourability criterion for bipartite graphs says that χ(G)≤2 exactly when G is a bipartite graph, and the odd-cycle characterization of bipartite graphs identifies the obstruction as an odd cycle. A nonempty graph with no edges has chromatic number one; a bipartite graph with at least one edge has chromatic number exactly two.
In the pairwise-conflict scheduling model of graph coloring, χ(G) is the least number of interchangeable slots needed. This turns a drawing into an optimization question: how many groups of compatible activities are unavoidable? Greedy coloring constructs a valid grouping quickly, but its number of colours can exceed the chromatic number.

Chromatic polynomial (PG​(t))

Words: 739 Articles: 3
Graph coloring OurBigBook.com
The chromatic polynomial turns a graph coloring problem into a counting problem: how many choices remain when adjacent vertices must have different colours? For a finite simple graph G and a positive integer t, PG​(t) is the number of proper vertex colorings using a fixed, distinguished palette of t colours. A colouring need not use every available colour, and exchanging two palette colours generally gives a different colouring. Although PG​ is a polynomial, its values at arbitrary noninteger arguments are not counts of colourings.
Consider the three-vertex path graph A--B--C. Choose A in t ways, then B in t−1 ways, then C in t−1 ways: A and C may agree because they are not adjacent. The multiplication principle gives
PP3​​(t)=t(t−1)2=t3−2t2+t.
(46)
Adding the edge AC makes the three-vertex complete graph K3​. Now C must avoid both preceding colours, so
PK3​​(t)=t(t−1)(t−2)=t3−3t2+2t.
(47)
With three available colours, the path graph has 12 colourings, whereas the triangle has 6. With two colours the counts are 2 and 0: the extra constraint makes the triangle impossible to colour.
For a nonempty graph, the chromatic number records only the first positive integer t for which PG​(t)>0. The chromatic polynomial also counts the choices for every larger palette. For the path the chromatic number is 2, and for the triangle it is 3. Counting assignments also gives a useful interpretation for scheduling: if adjacent vertices represent tasks that must use different slots, the chromatic polynomial counts the valid assignments to t named slots. Adding a conflict edge can only remove assignments.
The chromatic polynomial also remembers some of the graph's structure. For a simple graph with n≥1 vertices and m edges, its leading terms are tn−mtn−1; its degree of a polynomial gives the number of vertices, and its next coefficient gives the number of edges. It does not determine the graph completely. A four-vertex path graph and a four-vertex star graph are not related by a graph isomorphism, but both are trees and have chromatic polynomial t(t−1)3.
The early connection to map colouring appears in George D. Birkhoff's article [ref]. For a derivation of the counting recurrence and its leading coefficients, see Paul Johnson's MAS 341 lecture on chromatic polynomials.

Deletion-contraction recurrence for the chromatic polynomial (PG​(t)=PG−e​(t)−PG/e​(t))

Words: 253
Chromatic polynomial OurBigBook.com
Deleting an edge removes one colour constraint. Edge contraction describes exactly the newly admitted colourings that violate that constraint. If e joins distinct vertices u,v of a simple graph G, write G−e for the graph with that edge deleted and G/e for the graph with u,v identified and e removed. Parallel edges produced by the contraction may be reduced to one edge, since they impose the same condition on a proper vertex coloring. Then
PG​(t)=PG−e​(t)−PG/e​(t).
(48)
To see why, divide the proper vertex colorings of G−e into two classes. Those with different colours at u,v are exactly the colourings of G. Those with equal colours at u,v correspond one-to-one to colourings of G/e: the merged vertex receives their common colour. Subtracting the second class leaves the first.
For the triangle, delete AC to get a three-vertex path graph, or contract AC to get two vertices joined by an edge after removing the redundant parallel edge. Consequently,
PK3​​(t)=t(t−1)2−t(t−1)=t(t−1)(t−2).
(49)
At t=3, this says 6=12−6. Of the twelve path colourings pictured above, six give A,C the same colour; these are precisely the ones ruled out when we restore AC.
This recurrence is useful because it reduces a constrained counting problem to smaller graphs. A graph on n vertices with no edges has PG​(t)=tn, since every vertex chooses its colour independently. Repeated edge deletion and edge contraction reduce to this case and show that the counting function is a polynomial. The same recurrence gives its leading coefficients. The method is conceptually simple, although the number of recursive cases can still grow rapidly.

Chromatic polynomial after attaching a leaf

Words: 76
Chromatic polynomial OurBigBook.com
Attaching a new vertex that is a leaf of a graph multiplies the chromatic polynomial by t−1: after colouring the old graph, the new vertex may receive any colour except its neighbour's. Starting with one vertex and repeatedly adding a leaf of a graph constructs any finite tree. Thus a tree with n≥1 vertices has
PT​(t)=t(t−1)n−1.
(50)
In contrast, every pair of vertices in a complete graph must receive different colours, so the multiplication principle gives the falling factorial
PKn​​(t)=t(t−1)⋯(t−n+1).
(51)
For positive integers t<n this product vanishes, expressing the impossibility of assigning distinct colours to all n vertices.

Independent set (graph theory)

Words: 796 Articles: 8
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
An independent set selects mutually compatible objects when an edge of a graph represents a conflict. For example, if vertices are activities and edges join activities that cannot occur together, an independent set is a collection that can share one time slot. Finding the largest such collection is measured by the independence number.[ref]
In a finite simple graph G=(V,E), an independent set is a subset I⊆V with no edge joining two selected vertices:
u,v∈I, u=v⟹{u,v}∈/E.
(52)
The empty set and every singleton set are independent sets. In the cycle graph C5​ drawn under vertex cover, {0,2} is an independent set, but {0,4} is not: the closing edge 40 joins those two vertices. Choosing nonconsecutive labels is insufficient unless the wraparound edge is checked.
An independent set of maximum size has cardinality equal to the independence number. Being unable to add another vertex only makes an independent set inclusion-maximal. In the star graph K1,3​, the centre alone is inclusion-maximal, since it is adjacent to every leaf, but the three leaves form a larger independent set. This distinction mirrors the difference between an inclusion-minimal vertex cover and a minimum vertex cover.
Every independent set I has a vertex cover V∖I as its complement of a set; a largest independent set has a minimum vertex cover as its complement. In every proper vertex colouring, each colour class is an independent set, so graph coloring partitions the vertices into mutually compatible groups.

Independent transversal

Words: 78
Independent set (graph theory) OurBigBook.com
For a graph whose vertices are partitioned into parts, an independent transversal is an independent set containing exactly one vertex from each part. If a cycle's parts each have twelve vertices, choose one vertex uniformly and independently per part. A cycle edge joining distinct parts is selected at both ends with probability 1/144. Each event depends on at most 47 others, since each part meets at most 24 cycle edges. The Lovász local lemma applies because 48e/144<1, proving existence for an arbitrary such partition.

In each local term, all-zero neighbor assignment permits two choices at i, while every other assignment permits at most one. The maximum-entropy bound gives log2​(2bi​+1−1) for that term. Complete bipartite graphs Kd,d​ attain equality when one part is ordered before the other.

Independent set (graph theory) OurBigBook.com
The independence number is the largest cardinality of an independent set in a finite simple graph:
α(G)=max{∣I∣:I⊆V(G), I is an independent set of G}.
(53)
It answers "how many mutually compatible objects can be selected at once?", while the chromatic number asks how many compatible groups are needed for all the vertices. Diestel uses this notation for a largest independent set.[ref]
For the cycle graph C5​, the independent set {0,2} shows that α(C5​)≥2. Three selected vertices would require at least three unselected vertices separating them around the cycle graph, which has only five vertices. Thus α(C5​)=2. There are five largest independent sets, obtained by rotating {0,2} around the cycle graph, and five corresponding minimum vertex covers.
For the complete bipartite graph K2,3​, an independent set cannot contain a vertex from each side, since every such pair is joined by an edge. The larger side has three vertices, so α(K2,3​)=3. A triangle in a graph has independence number one. A graph with no edges and n vertices has independence number n, including α(G)=0 when n=0.
The complement correspondence between vertex covers and independent sets gives, with n=∣V(G)∣,
τ(G)+α(G)=n.
(54)
Every extra vertex that can be left in an independent set is one fewer vertex needed in a minimum vertex cover. This identity holds for all finite simple graphs, including the triangle in a graph and the cycle graph C5​; it does not require the bipartite graph hypothesis of Kőnig's theorem for bipartite matching.
For a nonempty graph, every colour class of a proper vertex colouring contains at most α(G) vertices. Counting all the vertices therefore gives

Since the chromatic number is an integer, the bound rounds up: for the cycle graph C5​, χ(C5​)≥⌈5/2⌉=3. It is attained by assigning colour A to 0,2, colour B to 1,3, and colour C to 4. All five edges, including 40, have differently coloured endpoints.

Hamilton cycle
Words: 892 Articles: 4
Cycle graph OurBigBook.com
A Hamilton cycle, also called a Hamiltonian cycle, is a cycle in a graph containing every vertex of the graph. Here the convention is a finite simple graph whose edges are undirected, with n=∣V∣≥3. A traversal is a sequence
v0​,v1​,…,vn−1​,vn​=v0​,
(58)
where v0​,…,vn−1​ are all the distinct vertices and {vi​,vi+1​}∈E for 0≤i<n. Thus "once" means once before the closing return: the start appears again at the end, and there are exactly n traversed edges. The graph may contain additional unused edges.[ref]
A Hamiltonian path visits all vertices once without requiring a return. Removing an edge from a Hamilton cycle gives a Hamiltonian path; a particular Hamiltonian path closes only if its endpoints are adjacent. An Euler circuit instead traverses every edge exactly once and can revisit vertices midway. The two requirements are independent, as these original labelled examples show.
For the complete graph K4​, use V={A,B,C,D} and E={AB,AC,AD,BC,BD,CD}, where AB abbreviates the unordered pair {A,B}. The route A,B,C,D,A is a Hamilton cycle: it visits every vertex and uses four of the six edges, omitting AC and BD. It is not an Euler circuit, and the graph admits no Euler circuit at all: every vertex degree is three, contradicting the Euler circuit criterion. The crossing of the drawn diagonals is not another vertex.
Conversely, take two triangles in a graph sharing only X, with V={X,A,B,C,D} and E={XA,AB,BX,XC,CD,DX}. The route X,A,B,X,C,D,X is an Euler circuit, using all six edges once; the vertex degrees are 4,2,2,2,2. It cannot be a Hamilton cycle, since X occurs midway as well as at the start and end. More strongly, no Hamilton cycle exists: X is a cut vertex, and deleting it leaves the two separate edges AB and CD. Nevertheless, A,B,X,C,D is a Hamiltonian path, whose endpoints are not adjacent.
