In the finite simple graph convention, Kn​ is a Hamiltonian graph for n≥3, because any ordering of its vertices closes using available edges.
Necessary conditions for a Hamilton cycle
Words: 142
Hamilton cycle OurBigBook.com
A Hamiltonian graph must be a connected graph and have minimum degree δ(G)≥2: each vertex has two distinct neighbours on its Hamilton cycle. It also has no cut vertex. Indeed, deleting any vertex from the Hamilton cycle leaves a graph path through every remaining vertex, so the remaining graph is connected. These are quick ways to rule out a Hamilton cycle.[ref]
Even these conditions together are not sufficient: the complete bipartite graph K2,3​ is connected, has minimum degree two and no cut vertex, but has no Hamilton cycle. Every graph cycle in a bipartite graph alternates between its two parts, using equally many vertices from each; it cannot use all two and all three.
In the other direction, Dirac's theorem gives a sufficient condition: a finite simple graph with n≥3 and δ(G)≥n/2 has a Hamilton cycle. Failure of this inequality proves nothing by itself: the cycle graph C5​ has a Hamilton cycle despite δ(C5​)=2<5/2.[ref]
Weighted Hamilton cycle (L(C)=∑e∈E(C)​we​)
Words: 344
Hamilton cycle OurBigBook.com
A weighted Hamilton cycle is a Hamilton cycle in a weighted graph, with cost equal to the sum of its traversed edge weights. Here weights represent symmetric nonnegative costs, rather than conductances. Asking whether a Hamilton cycle exists is a feasibility question; asking for the cheapest one is an instance of the travelling salesman problem. A complete graph supplies every possible connection between distinct vertices, making feasibility automatic for n≥3, while choosing the cheapest visiting order remains a separate mathematical optimization problem.
Assign the complete graph K4​ the symmetric edge costs wAB​=2, wBC​=3, wCD​=4, wAD​=5, wAC​=6 and wBD​=7, in arbitrary units. Fix the start at A and identify each Hamilton cycle with its reverse. The three possibilities are
A,B,C,D,AA,B,D,C,AA,C,B,D,A​:2+3+4+5=14,:2+7+4+6=19,:6+3+7+5=21.​
(59)
These exhaust the possibilities: the permutations of the other three vertices give 3!=6 orders, paired into three reversals. Hence the perimeter tour really is optimal for this toy instance. The diagram's geometric lengths are not costs, and no triangle inequality is assumed.
The usefulness of this model is to distinguish visiting required sites from covering required connections. If tasks are assigned to vertices and the route must return after one visit to each, a weighted Hamilton cycle captures the ordering requirement. If the job instead requires each edge once, the relevant object is an Euler circuit. The shortest path problem asks only for a cheapest route between specified endpoints. A 1954 primary research paper gave a concrete motivation for the travelling salesman problem: certify that a particular tour through 49 cities has minimum road-distance cost.[ref]
These are abstract route models. If a cost stands for a whole graph path through an underlying network, travelling between consecutive task vertices can pass through intermediate network vertices more than once. One visit per task therefore does not imply one visit per physical junction. One-way connections require a directed graph; changing costs or extra timing constraints require a richer model than the fixed symmetric toy instance.

Thus the value at a vertex is compared with its neighbours. Every row sums to zero, so L1=0: a constant vector produces no differences. This definition and the associated Graph Laplacian quadratic form are developed in Spielman's authored survey.[ref]
For the three-vertex path graph A−B−C, the vertex degrees are 1,2,1, and in that order

The constant eigenvector has eigenvalue zero; the other two describe progressively stronger neighbour disagreement. Dividing these eigenvectors by 3​,2​,6​, respectively, gives an orthonormal basis. The four-vertex cycle graph is already worked out under circulant matrix, where Fourier diagonalization of a circulant matrix gives its eigenvalues.
Every formula here uses L=D−A without degree normalization. For comparison, Chung's treatment uses the degree-scaled matrix D−1/2LD−1/2, with a convention for isolated vertices; its eigenvalues must not be substituted into the examples here.[ref]

Its kernel consists of vectors constant on each connected component of a graph after zero-weight edges are removed: an edge of weight zero imposes no constraint. In an electrical network, taking the weights to be electrical conductances makes xTLw​x the total power dissipated by Joule heating when x gives the voltages at the vertices. Conversely, these equalities make every entry of Lx zero. Thus the dimension of the kernel, equivalently the multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue, counts the connected components of a graph.

Flow network ((G,c,s,t))

A flow network is a directed graph G=(V,E) with distinct source and sink vertices s,t and a nonnegative flow network edge capacity cuv​ on each directed edge (u,v). In the finite setting here, every flow network edge capacity is a finite real number. A feasible flow assigns a nonnegative amount fuv​ to each original directed edge, satisfies the capacity constraints, and obeys flow conservation at every other vertex:
0≤fuv​≤cuv​,∑u:(u,v)∈E​fuv​=∑w:(v,w)∈E​fvw​(v∈/{s,t}).
(82)
These are nonnegative arc amounts. The antisymmetric convention in flow instead records net amounts θuv​=fuv​−fvu​, taking a missing arc amount as zero. The two conventions express the same flow conservation; keeping them distinct makes backward residual network edges easier to interpret.
Think of vertices as routers, directed edges as communication links, flow network edge capacities as available bandwidth, and flow as a steady transmission rate. An intermediate router can distribute incoming traffic among outgoing links, but flow conservation prevents it from creating traffic. The maximum flow problem asks how much total traffic can pass from s to t, allowing several graph paths to share the work. The same flow network language models transportation and abstract resource allocation.[ref]
Our running flow network has vertices V={s,a,b,t} and exactly five directed edges, with flow network edge capacities
(csa​,csb​,cab​,cat​,cbt​)=(3,2,1,2,3).
(83)
The cross edge a→b lets traffic entering a use spare capacity on b→t. With this edge removed, the two separate graph paths can carry only min(3,2)+min(2,3)=4; including it will let the maximum flow reach 5. Thus a link's usefulness depends on the rest of the flow network, rather than just its own flow network edge capacity.

A feasible flow and a cut of a flow network of equal value certify optimality without requiring a particular choice of augmenting paths.

(fsa​,fsb​,fab​,fat​,fbt​)=(3,2,1,2,3).

Every capacity constraint holds with equality. Flow conservation at a is 3=1+2, and at b it is 2+1=3. The strength of a flow is ∣f∣=3+2=5, also 2+3=5 entering t. Even a seemingly poor first augmenting path s→a→b→t, carrying 1, does not cause failure in this example. It leaves residual network capacity 2 along s→a→t and 2 along s→b→t. These two subsequent augmenting paths yield values 1, 3, and 5, and produce exactly the flow above. Backward residual network edges become essential in the unit-capacity example under residual network, where this same first choice blocks every unused forward route.
Discrete assignment is another reason to study maximum flow. Put unit-capacity edges from s to job vertices, from each job to eligible worker vertices, and from workers to t. An integral flow selects a matching in a graph: each job and worker participates at most once, and the strength of a flow counts assigned jobs. The integral max-flow theorem therefore turns maximum cardinality assignment into maximum flow. Minimizing assignment costs is the related assignment problem, modeled by minimum-cost flow.[ref]

The max-flow min-cut theorem identifies the minimum failure count λ. Unit-capacity vertex splitting also charges intermediary node failures. The network tolerates fewer than λ failures and fails for some set of λ failures. This concerns connection to at least one server, not separate connectivity to each server.

Edmonds–Karp algorithm

Words: 76
Maximum flow problem OurBigBook.com
This maximum flow algorithm repeatedly augments along a shortest residual path found by breadth-first search. Residual distances from the source never decrease. If the same arc becomes saturated again after being restored by a reverse augmentation, the distance to its tail has increased by at least two. Thus each arc is critical only O(∣V∣) times, yielding O(∣V∣∣E∣) augmentations. Each search costs O(∣E∣), so the total time is O(∣V∣∣E∣2). Termination with no residual source-sink path supplies a max-flow min-cut theorem certificate.

The maximum flow problem with internal vertex capacities reduces to the usual edge-capacitated problem by splitting each constrained vertex into input and output copies. The connecting edge carries its entire through-flow. Feasible flows correspond under this construction, preserving the source-to-sink value; the Ford-Fulkerson algorithm and max-flow min-cut theorem therefore apply to the transformed network.

This converts node-capacitated maximum flow to an ordinary flow network. For undirected mixed-failure cuts, normalize the source side so vout​ inside implies vin​ inside; then each original link contributes at most one crossing orientation.

Max-flow min-cut theorem (maxf​∣f∣=minS:s∈S,t∈/S​c(S,V∖S))

Words: 1k Articles: 12
Flow network OurBigBook.com
For a finite flow network with finite nonnegative real flow network edge capacities, the greatest strength of a flow of a feasible flow equals the least cut capacity of a source-to-sink cut of a flow network:
maxf feasible​∣f∣=minS⊆V:s∈S,t∈/S​∑(u,v)∈E:u∈S,v∈/S​cuv​.
(87)
For a maximum flow, the vertices reachable from the source in the residual network define a minimum cut whose outgoing original edges are saturated and whose incoming original edges carry zero flow.[ref]
Why is a cut of a flow network an upper bound? Sum flow conservation on its source side S. Internal edge contributions cancel, leaving
∣f∣=∑(u,v)∈E:u∈S,v∈/S​fuv​−∑(u,v)∈E:u∈/S,v∈S​fuv​≤∑(u,v)∈E:u∈S,v∈/S​cuv​=c(S,V∖S).
(88)
Only directed edges leaving S contribute to cut capacity. Directed edges entering S are subtracted in net flow, so adding their capacities to the upper bound would lose the intended bottleneck. This inequality is weak duality; the theorem says the bound is attained, an instance of strong duality. Its beauty is that a routing plan and a separating boundary independently witness each other's optimality.
In the running flow network, the two internal vertices give four possible source sides. For S={s}, the cut capacity is csa​+csb​=3+2=5. For S={s,a} it is csb​+cab​+cat​=2+1+2=5. For S={s,b} it is csa​+cbt​=3+3=6; the incoming edge a→b contributes nothing to that cut capacity. Finally, S={s,a,b} gives cat​+cbt​=2+3=5. Thus the minimum cut has cut capacity 5, matching the explicitly computed maximum flow.
Ford and Fulkerson's 1956 paper opens with a railway-capacity question attributed there to T. Harris and proves a minimal-cut theorem as Theorem 1. Its original formulation uses graph paths carrying nonnegative amounts; the residual reachability certificate for maximum flow below gives the finite directed flow network proof used here.[ref]

Residual reachability certificate for maximum flow

Words: 135
Max-flow min-cut theorem OurBigBook.com
In a finite flow network, a maximum flow exists because the feasible flow set contains the zero flow and is a compact set: the capacity constraints bound every coordinate, and they and flow conservation define a closed set. The strength of a flow is a continuous function, so the extreme value theorem gives an attained maximum. An augmenting path in the residual network would permit positive augmentation, contradicting maximality. The source-reachable vertices in the residual network therefore define a cut of a flow network whose outgoing original edges are saturated and incoming original edges carry zero flow. Flow conservation makes the strength of a flow equal to this cut capacity, proving the max-flow min-cut theorem.
Existence and strong duality for finite real flow network edge capacities do not imply finite termination for every choice of augmenting paths in the Ford-Fulkerson algorithm. With irrational capacities, some choices can continue forever. With integer capacities, Integrality of the Ford-Fulkerson algorithm instead forces finite termination; rational capacities reduce to that case by a common denominator. Choosing shortest augmenting paths as in the Edmonds–Karp algorithm avoids dependence on capacity magnitudes.[ref]

Uniform capacity perturbation of a flow network (v(ε)=minS​(c(S)+εm(S)))

Max-flow min-cut theorem OurBigBook.com
If every directed edge capacity increases by ε, a cut of a flow network with m(S) outgoing edges gains εm(S). By the max-flow min-cut theorem, the new maximum flow value is
v(ε)=minS:s∈S,t∈/S​(c(S)+εm(S)).
(89)
For a finite flow network, this is a nondecreasing concave piecewise-linear function, and its active cut can change as ε varies. Two unit-capacity edge-disjoint two-edge source-to-sink paths gain 2ε, refuting an invariably exact ε increase. If there is a directed source-to-sink path, every cut has at least one outgoing edge and the increase is at least ε; without a path it can be zero.

Residual network (Gf​)

Words: 653 Articles: 6
Max-flow min-cut theorem OurBigBook.com
For a feasible flow f, each original directed edge u→v supplies a forward residual network edge of capacity cuv​−fuv​ and a backward one v→u of capacity fuv​; zero-capacity residual edges may be omitted. The forward edge permits an increase, while the backward edge permits cancellation of existing flow. In particular, backward residual capacity is the amount already sent, rather than unused original capacity. If both original orientations exist, keep their residual contributions separate, or add capacities for contributions with the same direction. An augmenting path uses these permitted changes while preserving flow conservation and the capacity constraints.
To see why cancellation matters, give all five directed edges s→a, s→b, a→b, a→t, b→t unit flow network edge capacities. Starting from zero flow, an augmenting path s→a→b→t carrying 1 yields
(fsa​,fsb​,fab​,fat​,fbt​)=(1,0,1,0,1),∣f∣=1.
(90)
The remaining unused original edges are s→b and a→t, which do not form a source-to-sink graph path. However, the backward residual edge b→a has capacity fab​=1. Consequently the residual network contains the augmenting path s→b→a→t, with residual capacities 1,1,1.
Augment by 1: increase fsb​ and fat​ from 0 to 1, and decrease fab​ from 1 to 0. The result is
(fsa​,fsb​,fab​,fat​,fbt​)=(1,1,0,1,1),∣f∣=2.
(91)
Now flow conservation is 1=0+1 at a and 1+0=1 at b. The final flow sends one unit along each of s→a→t and s→b→t. The cut of a flow network S={s} has cut capacity 1+1=2, proving this is a maximum flow. Traversing b→a in the residual network revised the earlier routing decision; it did not send actual traffic along a nonexistent original edge.

On every source–sink cut, residual capacity is the original cut capacity minus the current net flow value f. Taking the minimum over cuts and applying the max-flow min-cut theorem to each network gives the displayed remaining-flow identity.

An augmenting path is a source-to-sink graph path P of positive capacities in the residual network. Its bottleneck is Δ=mine∈P​cf​(e)>0. Add Δ to original flow on forward residual edges and subtract Δ on backward residual edges. Each internal vertex still satisfies flow conservation, and the bottleneck guarantees every capacity constraint. The resulting feasible flow has strength of a flow ∣f∣+Δ. In the unit-capacity residual network example, Δ=1, and the subtraction on a→b is precisely what allows the value to rise from 1 to 2.

An augmenting path maximizing the possible increase in flow, namely its smallest residual network edge capacity. Eulerian graph

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
An Eulerian graph has an Euler circuit: a closed trail traversing every edge exactly once. Here the graph is a finite undirected graph, possibly a multigraph with self-loops. Parallel edges retain distinct identities, and each self-loop contributes two to its vertex degree. Repeated vertices are allowed. This models inspecting every road segment once, even when a junction must be revisited.
For a nonempty set of edges, the Euler circuit criterion requires a connected graph only on the edge support of a graph: isolated vertices impose no travel requirement. A single vertex with a self-loop and two vertices joined by two parallel edges are both Eulerian graphs. Neither requires three vertices. With no edges and at least one vertex, we allow the zero-length trail at that vertex as an Euler circuit; the graph with no vertices has no such walk.
The motivating Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem asks for an Eulerian trail, which need not return to its starting vertex. In Leonhard Euler's Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis by Leonhard Euler, §2 poses the bridge-crossing question and §§4–6 encode land regions by letters. The river's shape drops out: only the connections matter. The paper was written in 1735 and published in 1741, according to the Euler Archive; the journal volume carries the nominal year 1736.[ref]

Edge support of a graph (G+​)

Eulerian graph OurBigBook.com
For a finite undirected multigraph G=(V,E), its edge support of a graph is the subgraph G+​=(V+​,E) with V+​={v∈V:deg(v)>0}. It removes exactly the isolated vertices, retaining every edge, including self-loops and parallel edges. When E=∅, connectivity of this subgraph is the relevant condition for an Eulerian trail or Euler circuit.

Seven Bridges of Königsberg

Eulerian graph OurBigBook.com
Model the four land regions by vertices A,B,C,D and the seven bridges by distinct edges: two AB, two AC, and one each of AD,BD,CD. Their vertex degrees are (5,3,3,3). Leonhard Euler's paper records these connections in §6 and the obstruction in §9; §20 states the zero-or-two odd-region rule. Four odd vertex degrees exclude an Eulerian trail, even if returning to the starting vertex is optional.[ref]

Eulerian trail

Words: 264
Eulerian graph OurBigBook.com
An Eulerian trail, also called an Eulerian path, is a trail in a graph traversing every edge exactly once. The name Eulerian path does not require a graph path: vertices may repeat. A Hamiltonian path instead visits every vertex exactly once, and may omit edges. An Eulerian trail may omit isolated vertices, so these are different coverage requirements.
For a finite undirected multigraph with at least one edge, allowing self-loops, an Eulerian trail exists exactly when the edge support of a graph is a connected graph and there are zero or two vertices of odd vertex degree. In the two-odd-vertex case they must be the two distinct endpoints; in the zero-odd-vertex case every Eulerian trail is an Euler circuit. Count a self-loop twice in the vertex degree but once in the trail, and count each parallel edge separately.[ref]
The parity obstruction is local: each intermediate visit pairs an arriving edge with a departing edge. Only the distinct endpoints can have an unpaired incidence. The handshaking lemma, ∑v∈V​deg(v)=2∣E∣, also shows that the number of vertices with odd vertex degree is even. Sufficiency in the two-endpoint case reduces to the Euler circuit criterion: add one extra edge between the odd vertices, construct an Euler circuit, rotate its record to start with the extra edge, then delete that edge. The remaining trail has the required endpoints.
For the Seven Bridges of Königsberg multigraph, the vertex degrees at A,B,C,D are (5,3,3,3), so no Eulerian trail exists. Remove the unique edge AD: the vertex degrees become (4,3,3,2), and a six-edge Eulerian trail runs from B to C. Label the parallel edges p1​,p2​ between A,B and q1​,q2​ between A,C; label BD by r and CD by s. A complete record is B,p1​,A,q1​,C,s,D,r,B,p2​,A,q2​,C. It revisits A,B,C while using every remaining edge once.

Euler circuit

Words: 157
Eulerian graph OurBigBook.com
An Euler circuit, also called an Euler tour, is an Eulerian trail whose final vertex equals its initial vertex. Its length is ∣E∣. It can revisit other vertices, unlike a Hamiltonian cycle, which visits each vertex once before returning to the start. For a finite undirected multigraph with at least one edge, an Euler circuit exists exactly when the edge support of a graph is a connected graph and every vertex degree is even.
For example, let p,q be distinct parallel edges joining A,B, let ℓ be a self-loop at A, and add an isolated vertex Z. Then (deg(A),deg(B),deg(Z))=(4,2,0), and A,ℓ,A,p,B,q,A is an Euler tour. The self-loop supplies one traversal and two incidences; Z need not be visited. Replacing p,q by a single edge changes both vertex degrees to odd numbers and removes the possibility of an Euler circuit. Thus collapsing parallel edges can change the answer.
Two triangles in a graph sharing one vertex A give another instructive Euler circuit: A,B,C,A,D,E,A. The shared vertex has vertex degree four, the others have vertex degree two, and A is revisited between the two closed trails. This is precisely the splice used by Hierholzer's algorithm.

Euler circuit criterion

Words: 376 Articles: 1
Eulerian graph OurBigBook.com
Let G=(V,E) be a finite undirected multigraph, allowing self-loops and distinct parallel edges, with E=∅. Then
G has an Euler circuit⟺G+​ is connected and deg(v)≡0(mod2) for every v∈V,
(93)
where G+​ is the edge support of a graph, and vertex degrees count each self-loop twice. There is no lower bound of three on the number of vertices. If E=∅, the zero-length convention gives an Euler circuit exactly when V=∅.[ref]
The two requirements are independent: two separate vertices, each carrying a self-loop, have even vertex degrees but disconnected edge support of a graph, so no Euler circuit can cover both edges.
Necessity follows because a single trail cannot cover edges in different connected components of a graph, while a closed trail pairs all arriving and departing incidences, including those at its starting vertex. For sufficiency, extend a trail using unused edges until no extension is possible. Even vertex degree parity prevents it from stopping anywhere except its starting vertex: a different stopping vertex would have an odd number of used incidences and hence at least one unused incidence. The result is a closed trail.
If unused edges remain, connectivity of the edge support of a graph supplies a vertex on the current closed trail with an unused incident edge. Removing a closed trail leaves even unused vertex degrees, so the same argument constructs another closed trail from that vertex. Splice it into the existing record. The two trails use disjoint edge identities, so the splice repeats no edge. Each splice uses more edges; finiteness ensures termination with an Euler circuit. This is the constructive idea of Hierholzer's algorithm.
In the drawing, arrows indicate the chosen traversal direction along undirected edges. The first closed trail uses AB,BC,CA and the second uses AD,DE,EA. Insert the second at the final occurrence of A in A,B,C,A, giving A,B,C,A,D,E,A. A reader can check consecutive endpoints, closure, and the six distinct edges directly. With multigraphs, perform the same check on edge identities, since endpoint pairs alone cannot distinguish parallel edges.

Hierholzer's algorithm

Words: 58
Euler circuit criterion OurBigBook.com
Hierholzer's algorithm constructs an Euler circuit by growing closed trails along unused edges and splicing them at shared vertices, as in the Euler circuit criterion. Each edge must have a distinct record. An implementation using adjacency lists, a stack, and a used flag for each edge runs in O(∣V∣+∣E∣) time, including the connectivity and vertex degree checks. Store both incidences of a self-loop, while marking its single edge record used only once.

Planar graph

Words: 2k Articles: 29
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A planar graph admits at least one graph drawing in which edges meet only at common endpoints. This is a property of the abstract graph, not a requirement on every graph drawing. A plane graph specifies one such drawing.[ref]
For example, the complete graph K4​ joins every pair of four vertices, giving six edges. Put its vertices at the corners of a square and its diagonals cross. Instead put A,B,C at the corners of a triangle and D inside it: the same six edges AB,AC,BC,AD,BD,CD now meet only at their endpoints. The first graph drawing obscures planarity; the second proves it. In particular, its crossing number is zero.
The distinction matters whenever connections must fit on one surface without intersecting. A failed graph drawing may only need rearrangement, whereas nonplanarity by edge counts proves that every rearrangement fails.

A finite simple graph is a planar graph if and only if it contains no graph subdivision of the complete graph K5​ or the complete bipartite graph K3,3​ as a subgraph; equivalently, neither is a topological minor. The easy direction follows by tracing each replacement graph path as one drawn edge. The converse asserts that every failure of planarity contains one of these two patterns.[ref]
Graph Theory by Reinhard Diestel (Planar Graphs preview, §4.4, Theorem 4.4.6, printed p. 111) dates Kuratowski's theorem to 1930 and the equivalent graph minor characterization to 1937. These dates are that textbook's historical attribution.

Its independent bond percolation threshold is 1/2​, as follows from three-terminal cell partition duality.

Five color theorem

Planar graph OurBigBook.com
Every finite planar graph admits a proper vertex coloring with at most five colors. Euler formula for a connected planar graph supplies a vertex of degree at most five. Inductively color its deletion. The only obstruction is five differently colored neighbours in cyclic order. If opposite neighbours 1 and 3 are in different two-color components, interchange one component. If they are connected, planarity prevents opposite neighbours 2 and 4 from being connected in their two-color subgraph, and that interchange frees a color instead. This is a Kempe chain proof.

Bipartite graph

Words: 2k Articles: 15
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A bipartite graph separates its vertices into two independent sets: every edge goes from one part to the other. Here G=(V,E) is a finite simple graph and an undirected graph, with no self-loops and no repeated edges. The two parts X,Y⊆V satisfy
X∩Y=∅,X∪Y=V,{u,v}∈E⟹(u∈X, v∈Y) or (u∈Y, v∈X).
(104)
Thus neither part contains an edge. The parts need not have equal sizes, and some pairs across them may have no edge; requiring every cross pair gives a complete bipartite graph. The independent set and cross-edge definitions are equivalent.[ref]
For example, the six-vertex cycle graph C6​ with edges 12,23,34,45,56,61 has parts X={1,3,5} and Y={2,4,6}. Drawing the same graph as a hexagon or in two columns changes neither its edges nor its bipartite property. An extra isolated vertex z can go in either part.
We allow either part to be empty. Consequently a graph with no edges is bipartite, even when V=∅; choose X=V, Y=∅. Here "two colours" means two colours are available, with no requirement to use both. This convention explicitly includes the empty case, whereas definitions requiring two nonempty classes need an exception. For several connected components of a graph, choose the two parts separately in each graph component and take their unions. In a nonempty connected graph that is bipartite, fixing one vertex's colour forces all others along graph paths, so its two-colour assignment is unique up to swapping the colours. Each graph component, including an isolated vertex, can be swapped independently.
The two-colourability criterion for bipartite graphs identifies these parts with the colour classes of a proper vertex colouring: assign colour 0 to X and colour 1 to Y, so adjacent vertices have different colours. More surprisingly, the odd-cycle characterization of bipartite graphs turns a global requirement into one precise obstruction:
G is bipartite⟺G contains no odd cycle.
(105)
This statement is for the finite undirected graph and simple graph model above; a graph cycle has distinct vertices except for the repeated starting vertex. Along a graph cycle in a bipartite graph, colours alternate, so returning to the starting colour takes an even number of edges. Therefore any odd cycle, whether or not other edges join its vertices, prevents a bipartite split.[ref]
Breadth-first search supplies the converse constructively. Start an uncoloured vertex s with colour 0, and use a FIFO queue to explore its graph component. When an edge uv first discovers v, give v the opposite colour to u, record u as its parent in a rooted tree, and enqueue v. If both endpoints of any scanned edge already have the same colour, stop with a conflict. Restart from an uncoloured vertex until every graph component has been examined. If no conflict occurs, all edges cross the two colour classes, which are the required independent sets.[ref]
A conflict also explains the failure. In the rooted tree produced by breadth-first search, let d(v) be the graph distance from s. The colour of v is its distance's integer parity. An edge uv in an undirected graph satisfies ∣d(u)−d(v)∣≤1, so equal colours force d(u)=d(v). Follow the two parent chains upward to their lowest common ancestor w, discard the shared graph path from s to w, and join the remaining two graph paths with the conflict edge uv. The result is a genuine graph cycle with
(d(u)−d(w))+(d(v)−d(w))+1=2(d(u)−d(w))+1
(106)
edges, an odd integer. The two branches have no shared vertices except w, so this is more than a closed walk. This odd cycle is a certificate that anyone can check directly, using only its listed vertices and edges.
In the example, breadth-first search from s gives d(w)=1, d(a)=d(b)=2, and d(u)=d(v)=3. The conflict edge uv closes the odd cycle w,a,u,v,b,w, with five edges. The common edge sw is excluded. Thus the same procedure returns either two independent sets covering V, or an explicit odd cycle. With adjacency lists and constant-time FIFO queue operations, its time complexity is O(∣V∣+∣E∣) in Big O notation, with O(∣V∣) additional storage.[ref]
The two parts often have a practical meaning: workers and jobs, with an edge exactly when a worker can perform a job. A matching in a graph chooses compatible worker–job pairs with no reused endpoint; merely being bipartite does not guarantee enough compatible pairs. Hall's marriage theorem characterizes when every worker can be matched, and the assignment problem adds costs to seek an optimal assignment. These connections make the bipartite structure useful after recognition, as the starting point for selecting edges under constraints.

If the endpoints of an edge rank one another last and one stable matching in a bipartite graph contains that edge, every stable matching contains it. In the symmetric difference of two stable matchings, preference comparisons propagate along alternating paths: if a vertex prefers its new partner, that partner must prefer its old partner to avoid blocking the old matching. An alternating path cannot end unmatched on the preferred side, so the component is an alternating cycle, on which the two parts prefer opposite matchings. A mutual-worst edge absent from the new matching would make both its endpoints prefer the new matching, contradicting this propagation.

Gale-Shapley algorithm

Words: 79
Stable matching in a bipartite graph OurBigBook.com
An unmatched vertex in the proposing part proposes to its best untried neighbour. The receiving vertex keeps its preferred proposal, rejecting any other. There are at most as many proposals as edges, so this terminates. A rejected proposer can never become preferable to the receiver's final partner, since the receiver's held partner only improves. An edge never proposed along cannot block either: its proposer finishes with a better partner or has exhausted all choices. Thus the final matching in a graph is stable.

Perfect matching

Words: 369 Articles: 3
Matching (graph theory) OurBigBook.com
A perfect matching is a matching in a graph that covers every vertex exactly once. Its edges have no shared endpoints, and every vertex is an endpoint of one selected edge. It is useful when a collection must be divided into disjoint pairs with no element left over.
In a bipartite graph with equally many vertices on its two sides, a perfect matching can assign every person one allowed job and every job one person. The example under permanent of a matrix has three people and three jobs, with exactly three valid assignments. The blue edges below show those three perfect matchings; a crossing in the drawing is not an extra vertex.
Every selected edge covers two vertices, so a graph with an odd integer number of vertices has no perfect matching. An even integer number is necessary but does not guarantee existence: an isolated vertex cannot be covered. A perfect matching also need not be unique. For example, the complete bipartite graph K2,2​ has two perfect matchings, corresponding to the two ways of assigning two people to two jobs.
Counting all perfect matchings is a different question from finding one. For a zero-one biadjacency matrix of a balanced bipartite graph, the count is its permanent of a matrix. The nonzero determinant criterion for a perfect matching supplies an existence test, but cancellation means that a zero determinant does not rule one out.

Uniform linearized chord diagram
Words: 129
Linearized chord diagram model OurBigBook.com
Pair 2n linearly ordered endpoints uniformly. Each pair is a chord; its larger endpoint ends a vertex block, with all endpoints after the previous right endpoint merged into that vertex. Orient the chord from its right-endpoint block to its left-endpoint block. Removing the last endpoint and its mate leaves a uniform smaller pairing. Reinserting the mate into one of 2n−1 equally likely gaps chooses an existing block proportionally to its endpoint count, or the final gap creates a self-loop. This proves equivalence with the linearized chord diagram model.
An equivalent continuous representation draws n independent pairs of independent uniform points on [0,1], orders the pairs by their maxima R1​<⋯<Rn​, and calls their minima Li​. The Ri2​ are uniform order statistics; conditional on all the Ri​, the Li​ are independent uniform points on [0,Ri​].

The Rado graph is the unique countably infinite graph with the two-uniform hypergraph extension property. Equivalently, for any disjoint finite vertex sets U,W, some new vertex is adjacent to every member of U and no member of W. The back-and-forth method proves uniqueness. Continuity of fixed-choice percolation

Words: 109
Achlioptas process OurBigBook.com
A fixed-choice Achlioptas process cannot have its largest component of a graph jump from o(n) to a fixed positive fraction of n within o(n) steps, with high probability. The proof combines forced merging of large components and persistence of unsampled graph components. An assumed jump forces positive vertex mass in each band [k,Dk) slightly before the jump: insufficient smaller components can feed the final large component, while enough components above Dk would merge too early. Persistence carries a fixed positive amount of each band to a common time. Taking sufficiently many disjoint bands with k=1,D,D2,… then counts more than n vertices. The number of offered candidates is fixed throughout this argument. Riordan and Warnke establish this obstruction and broader continuity results in their original research paper.

This is a deliberately nonoptimal positive constant.

For sufficiently large n, (1−3w/n)2T≥e−16BD, so the expected value of the untouched vertex mass Y is at least αe−16BDn. Replacing one row of two candidate edges can change Y by at most 8Dk, because only the initial graph components hit by an old or new endpoint can change status. The McDiarmid inequality therefore makes Y≥αe−16BDn/2 except on an event of probability e−cn/k, for a positive constant c depending only on α,B,D. An untouched graph component stays unchanged whichever offered edge is selected.
For candidates restricted to absent edges, generate each by an independent uniform proposal stream and reject already present edges. During any interval of O(n) steps with O(n) present edges, each proposal has rejection probability O(1/n) conditional on the past. The number of rejections is at most O(logn) except on an event of probability smaller than any inverse power of n: if there were r rejections among 2T+r proposals, a union bound over their positions bounds this by (r2T+r​)(C/n)r. The first 2T proposals are independent and give the previous untouched-mass estimate. Extra proposals can touch at most 2r additional initial graph components, losing only O(Dklogn)=o(n) vertices for fixed k. This leaves the stated βn bound. A union bound makes these estimates simultaneous over starting times m≤3n. They hold through the entire interval, so deterministic or random stopping times within it are allowed.

Complement graph

Words: 78 Articles: 1
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The complement of a simple graph has exactly the edges absent from the original graph; a vertex of degree d acquires degree n−1−d.

Simultaneously bipartite graph and complement

Words: 54
Complement graph OurBigBook.com
If a graph and its complement graph are both bipartite, then the graph has at most four vertices. Indeed, each part of a bipartition of the original graph induces a clique in the complement and therefore has at most two vertices. The bound is attained by the four-vertex path, whose complement is another four-vertex path.

Menger theorem

Words: 650 Articles: 17
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The maximum number of disjoint paths joining two vertex sets equals the minimum size of a separating set, with vertex and edge versions according to the chosen notion of disjointness.

Vertex separator

Words: 26
Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
An x-y vertex separator is a set of vertices, excluding x and y, whose deletion leaves no path from x to y.

Local connectivity (κ(a,b;G))

Words: 39
Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
For nonadjacent vertices a,b of a graph G, their local connectivity κ(a,b;G) is the minimum size of an a-b vertex separator. By the Menger theorem, it also equals the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint a-b paths.

Internally vertex-disjoint paths

Words: 13
Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
Paths with common endpoints are internally vertex-disjoint when they share no other vertex.

Set version of Menger theorem

Words: 75 Articles: 1
Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
For vertex sets A,B, the maximum number of pairwise vertex-disjoint A-B paths equals the minimum size of a vertex set meeting every A-B path.

Fan lemma

Words: 46
Set version of Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
In a k-connected graph, for a vertex x and a set Y of at least k other vertices, there are k paths from x to distinct vertices of Y that meet only at x. This follows from the Set version of Menger theorem by separating x from Y.

Linked graph

Words: 218 Articles: 2
Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
A graph is k-linked when any 2k distinct vertices paired as (xi​,yi​) can be joined by k mutually vertex-disjoint paths from xi​ to yi​.
Unlike vertex connectivity, linkage specifies all endpoint pairings simultaneously.

Four-connected planar obstruction to two-linkage

Words: 87
Linked graph OurBigBook.com
On vertices 0,…,7, join cyclic indices differing by one or two modulo eight. The resulting planar graph has a square face bounded in order by 0,2,4,6. Deleting at most three vertices cannot disconnect it: each break in the surviving cyclic chain requires two consecutive deleted vertices, and two separate breaks require four deletions. It is therefore four-connected. Disjoint paths joining 0 to 4 and 2 to 6 would cross in the complementary disk of the square face, contrary to the Jordan curve theorem. Thus four-connectivity does not guarantee two-linkage.

Rooted dense minor linkage (2δ(H)≥∣H∣+4k−1)

Words: 97
Linked graph OurBigBook.com
If a graph is 2k-connected and has a graph minor H satisfying 2δ(H)≥∣H∣+4k−1, it is k-linked. Write d=∣H∣−1−δ(H), so ∣H∣≥2d+4k+1. The rooted branch-set reduction replaces the minor model by ∣H∣−k disjoint connected sets, the first 2k containing any prescribed terminals separately, each missing at most d of the remaining sets. Every prescribed pair then has at least k+1 common adjacent unused sets, allowing the k connections to be selected successively. The reduction uses rooted separations of a graph, contraction of edges outside distinct branch sets, and a final Hall marriage theorem matching; the separation condition prevents a contraction from destroying access to the model.

Vertex connectivity

Words: 189 Articles: 5
Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
Vertex connectivity κ(G) is the smallest number of vertices whose deletion disconnects a nontrivial graph or reduces it to one vertex.

Rooted separation of a graph

Words: 77
Vertex connectivity OurBigBook.com
For a specified set S of vertices, a rooted separation is a pair (A,B) with A∪B=V(G), S⊆A, and no edges between A∖B and B∖A. Its order is ∣A∩B∣. It avoids a branch set C when A∩C=∅. A graph with vertex connectivity at least ∣S∣ has no rooted separation of order below ∣S∣ avoiding a nonempty branch set: both sides of such a separation would be nonempty after deleting its separator.

k-connected graph (k-connected graph)

Words: 91 Articles: 3
Vertex connectivity OurBigBook.com
A graph with more than k vertices is k-connected when deleting fewer than k vertices always leaves it connected, equivalently when its vertex connectivity is at least k.
Dirac circumference theorem
Words: 43 Articles: 1
k-connected graph OurBigBook.com
A k-connected graph has a cycle of length at least min{∣G∣,2k}.
Longest-cycle attachment argument
Words: 30
Dirac circumference theorem OurBigBook.com
A component outside a longest cycle has at least k attachment vertices in a k-connected graph, and no two attachments are consecutive, forcing cycle length at least 2k.
3-connected graph
Words: 20
k-connected graph OurBigBook.com
A graph is 3-connected when it has at least four vertices and remains connected after deletion of any two vertices.

Edge connectivity

Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
Edge connectivity λ(G) is the smallest number of edges whose deletion disconnects the graph.

Whitney inequalities for graph connectivity

Words: 46 Articles: 1
Menger theorem OurBigBook.com
For every nontrivial graph, κ(G)≤λ(G)≤δ(G).
These compare two numerical invariants of connectivity with the minimum degree of a graph.

Connectivity realization construction

Words: 31
Whitney inequalities for graph connectivity OurBigBook.com
Two large cliques joined by a bipartite cross graph with edge count ℓ and vertex-cover number k realize edge connectivity ℓ and vertex connectivity k while preserving a chosen minimum degree.

Graph subdivision (TH)

Words: 301 Articles: 3
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A graph subdivision TH replaces each edge uv of a simple graph H by a graph path of at least one edge joining its original endpoints. The original vertices are branch vertices of a graph subdivision. The replacement graph paths have pairwise disjoint interiors, contain no branch vertices of a graph subdivision internally, and together make up the entire new graph. Leaving an edge unchanged is allowed.[ref]
For an explicit example, take H with vertex set {A,B,C,D} and edges AB,BC,CA,AD: a triangle in a graph with one attached leaf of a graph. Replace its edges by the following branch paths of a graph subdivision:
PAB​=(A,x,B),PBC​=(B,y,z,C),PCA​=(C,A),PAD​=(A,D).
(128)
The resulting graph subdivision S has vertex set {A,B,C,D,x,y,z} and edges Ax,xB,By,yz,zC,CA,AD. The internal vertex sets are {x},{y,z},∅,∅, so disjointness is explicit. The degrees of vertices of A,B,C,D remain 3,2,2,1, respectively; the three new internal vertices each have degree of a vertex two.
Adding m internal vertices to a finite graph increases both its vertex count and its edge count by m. Here m=3, so four vertices and four edges become seven of each; the graph excess is unchanged. Each replacement graph path remains a route between the same junctions. Thus graph subdivision preserves whether a graph is a planar graph: insert intermediate vertices along a crossing-free drawing, or trace each replacement graph path as one edge to recover a drawing of the original graph. Travel times or capacities are separate modelling choices and are not determined by this adjacency construction.

Branch vertex of a graph subdivision

Words: 52
Graph subdivision OurBigBook.com
A branch vertex of a graph subdivision is a retained original vertex in a specified graph subdivision. Its degree of a vertex in that graph subdivision equals its original degree of a vertex. It need not have degree of a vertex at least three: B,C,D in the example are also branch vertices of a graph subdivision. When the target itself has vertices of degree of a vertex two, adjacency alone need not identify which vertices were original; the specified target mapping supplies that distinction.

Branch path of a graph subdivision

Words: 21
Graph subdivision OurBigBook.com
A branch path of a graph subdivision is the replacement graph path for one original edge. Its endpoints are the corresponding branch vertices of a graph subdivision; its internal vertices have degree of a vertex two within the graph subdivision.

Complete graph subdivision (TKr​)

Words: 23
Graph subdivision OurBigBook.com
A TKr​ is a subdivision of the complete graph Kr​. Its original complete-graph vertices are branch vertices and its replaced edges are branch paths.

Bipartite vertex cover

Words: 30
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
König's theorem equates the minimum vertex-cover size of a bipartite graph with its maximum matching size.
A bipartite vertex cover is a vertex cover restricted to a bipartite graph; Kőnig's theorem for bipartite matching computes its minimum size.

Erdős-Gallai theorem

Words: 22
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
The Erdős-Gallai theorem characterizes which finite nonincreasing sequences of nonnegative integers form the degree sequence of a simple graph, using an even total degree and partial-sum inequalities.

Prism graph

Words: 21
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A prism graph joins two copies of a cycle graph by matching corresponding vertices. The triangular prism graph is the three-cycle case, with six vertices and nine edges.

Squaregraph

Words: 44
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A squaregraph has a plane embedding in which every bounded face has four sides and every interior vertex has degree at least four. Its outer face may have more than four sides, so this definition differs from a planar quadrangulation requiring every face to have degree four.

Vertex cycle cover

Words: 29
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A vertex cycle cover is a collection of cycles whose union contains every vertex of a graph; its cycles can overlap. A cycle cover of a directed graph additionally requires directed, vertex-disjoint cycles, and a spanning circuit family can allow overlaps.

Pósa's theorem

Words: 26
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
Pósa's theorem gives a sufficient degree-sequence condition for a Hamiltonian cycle in a finite simple graph. Longest-path rotation is a technique used in proving Hamiltonicity results; it is not itself the degree-sequence theorem.

Pseudoforest

Words: 39
Graph theory OurBigBook.com
A pseudoforest is an undirected graph in which every connected component of a graph contains at most one cycle in a graph. Thus each component is a tree or a unicyclic component. A finite tree component has one fewer edge than vertices; a finite unicyclic component has equally many edges and vertices.
